title_zh: Trump wooed Latino voters, but his ICE tactics sent them back to the polls: ‘They’re taking our neighbors’

Texas business owner says he expected ICE raids to focus on those with criminal records not his relatives and employees

T uesday night’s explosive rout of the Republican party was supercharged by the fury of Hispanic Americans who turned out in record numbers in key battlegrounds to protest the Trump administration ’s anti-immigrant assault on their communities.
“Trump went against us,” said Benny Melendez from Weslaco, Texas . “He made us the target of ICE operations, so we decided to punish him by voting against his party. That’s what happened.”

Melendez, the owner of a small housebuilding company in south Texas, voted for Donald Trump in the presidential election two years ago, attracted by his promise to secure the Mexican border and improve the economy. But on Tuesday, he cast his vote for the Democrats in a display of pure anger.

Two of his cousins and up to 15 of his building workers have been picked up and deported to Mexico by ICE . When Melendez voted for Trump in 2024 he expected the immigration raids would focus on those with criminal records, he said, not his relatives and employees.
“They’re taking our neighbors. They’re taking our friends. They’re they’re taking our workers, and they’re taking our family members. This is an attack against our community.”

Melendez’s rage, replicated in the millions across Texas, Florida and other critical swing states, itself tells a story. It speaks to how Trump first wooed, and then alienated, the backing of many Latino voters, effectively shooting himself in the foot.
In the closing days of the 2024 presidential race, Trump made a special pitch to Hispanic voters. “I love Hispanics,” he told them , “and Hispanics love Trump.”
To some extent, that audacious appeal worked: in 2024 Trump garnered 48% of the Latino vote, according to Pew Research , 12 points up from four years previously.

But on Tuesday night, Latino voters delivered Trump a resounding message of a very different sort. In a dizzying switch in affiliation, Hispanic American support for Republicans plummeted from the almost half who backed Trump just two years ago to 30% today.

According to the New York Times analysis of voter trends, election night marked a 28 point shift from 2024 in Latino allegiance toward Democrats nationwide. The dramatic turn was more notable than any other demographic voting group, with the next largest shift of 17% coming from Asian Americans.
The shift helped propel Democratic wins in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, as well as governor’s seats in states like Texas, Georgia, Arizona and Nevada.
If Trump and the Republican party had assumed they had forged a new alignment with Hispanic voters, they must now think again. Any such alliance was abruptly and spectacularly uncoupled on Tuesday.
“People have called us the sleeping giant for a long time, and now we’re really the swinging giant,” said Stephanie Valencia, co-founder of the Latino polling experts, Equis Research.
“The vociferous message that voters sent last night was an F-U to Trump and Republicans and their misplaced priorities and broken promises.”

It was a night of stunning surprises, and of firsts. Texas, the state with the second largest Hispanic populace after California, elected its first Latino governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa , a native of the Rio Grande Valley whose mother is an immigrant from Mexico, in an astounding rebuke to decades of largely white Republican rule.
Democrat Xavier Becerra, the son of immigrants from Mexico, will become the first elected Latino governor in California, the world’s fourth largest economy.

Here too the same voters’ fury was powerfully vented. “We’ve known better than anybody what these last two years have been like,” California senator Alex Padilla, the son of Mexican immigrants, told the crowd at Becerra’s closing campaign stop at the Palladium in Los Angeles on Sunday. “We have endured relentless attacks on our communities by Donald Trump and his rogue ICE agents.”

In his first public appearance after an election that soundly repudiated his policies, President Donald Trump turned to a topic both familiar and, given the context, surprising
By GARY FIELDS Associated Press and LISA MASCARO Associated Press

WASHINGTON -- In his first public appearance after an election that soundly repudiated his policies, President Donald Trump turned to a topic both familiar and, given the context, surprising: not his policies or politics, but his efforts to remake pieces of the city that is the backdrop to his presidency.

Despite Trump’s affinity for project management, though, with Democrats taking control of Congress, the work the administration is doing to change the physical face of the District of Columbia is sure to face far more roadblocks than it did for the first two years of his second term.

From the renaming of and renovation plans for the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and erecting an arch 100 feet (30.48 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty without its pedestal, the president has been deeply involved in how D.C. looks. Democrats have voiced opposition but, in terms of power, have been in the wilderness.

The potential collision point between an oppositional oversight from Democrats and the president's preoccupation with the projects was evident in his last message to the American public before the election — and in his first afterward, too.

Both focused to some degree on his projects. On Monday, it was the reflecting pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial ; on Wednesday, it was a tour of the under-construction White House ballroom, where he talked columns and steel beams and Corinthian designs.

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee with jurisdiction over the Interior Department that is involved with operations at parks and federal lands, spent much of the past year probing and questioning Trump’s projects, laying the groundwork for this moment.

“We’ve pushed back against vanity projects that seek to transform treasured public spaces into gaudy tributes to Trump. We exposed corruption, uncovered the efforts to hijack America’s 250th birthday, demanded accountability, and offered a compelling alternative governing vision grounded in science, fairness, environmental responsibility, and the rule of law,” Huffman said in a letter to colleagues seeking their support to be chairman.

As chairman with a strong Democratic majority, “I will ensure that the Committee’s full investigative and oversight authority is leveraged to uncover wrongdoing, demand accountability, and protect the public interest," he said.

Trump has been rushing the various projects, a point Virginia Democratic Rep. Don Beyer made Thursday at a public hearing when he opposed construction of the memorial arch the president has planned in Memorial Circle directly across the Memorial Bridge from the Lincoln Memorial.
"The appropriations process beginning Jan. 3 will be controlled by Democrats. That will be one of the ways Congressman Beyer will step in,” said Beyer’s spokesman Aaron Fritschner.
A less appreciated impact will be the change in who names the general counsel of the House. The House Speaker has that role, presumably Rep. Hakeem Jeffries.

While Democrats have joined in lawsuits opposing the various projects, their filings don't carry the weight of Congress as the minority. “You’ll see the new majority pulling back the balance of power that (House Speaker) Mike Johnson was willing to cede,” Fritschner said.

Beyer has already been a critic, Fritschner said, and cited other members who have signed on in amicus briefs. More than 120 witnesses were on hand for the National Capital Planning Commission meeting, which ran for 9 ½ hours late into Thursday night.

The commission gave the 250-foot (76-meter) arch its final approval on an 8-4 vote, before a federal judge stepped in before midnight to block the Trump administration from breaking ground for 14 days.

title_en: Judge temporarily halts building work on Trump’s triumphal arch
title_zh: Judge temporarily halts building work on Trump’s triumphal arch
summary: Federal judge issues 14-day restraining order on any construction work on Washington monument, hours after it was approved by planning commission A federal judge has halted construction work on Donald Trump’s towering triumphal arch for 14 days, a major setbac

body_en: Judge temporarily halts building work on Trump’s triumphal arch | Washington DC
Federal judge issues 14-day restraining order on any construction work on Washington monument, hours after it was approved by planning commission

A federal judge has halted construction work on Donald Trump’s towering triumphal arch for 14 days, a major setback for one of the president’s most prominent projects in his vision to remake Washington.

The temporary restraining order was issued by US district judge Tanya Chutkan in the early hours of Friday. It followed a series of steps taken on Thursday by the government, including the final approval of the 250-foot-high (76-meter) arch by the National Capital Planning Commission in an 8-4 vote after a nine-hour hearing where dozens of witnesses opposed the construction.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats gained control of Congress.
DoJ says Trump’s proposed 250ft arch would be completed after end of his term

The administration had said the work on the arch could begin as soon as the approval and the interior department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.

In issuing the delay, Chutkan granted the request of the latest plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch. Chutkan also consolidated lawsuits from the District of Columbia and Virginia with a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian.
It’s unclear how much the project will cost, or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100m.

The vote by the planning commission on Thursday came after nine and a half hours and scores of people opposing it. The vote by the commission broke along federal and local lines. Those in favor work for the administration or are connected to the president, who was pushing for the immediate construction. Opponents represented the city of Washington.

The remote, call-in hearing – which crashed repeatedly in the first few hours and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section – drew witnesses who gave impassioned comments opposing an arch that they said would destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington national cemetery, where hundreds of thousands of fallen service members and military veterans are buried.
The panel’s Trump-appointed chair launched the meeting with a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission’s chair.

As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget.

Commissioner Paul Ingrassia, a lawyer for the General Services Administration, said the arch was “not about politics. It’s about remembrance. It’s about celebrating our history. It’s about commemorating veterans. And it’s really something that’s a noble tribute to our nation and something that we can all rally behind.”

But DC city council member Phil Mendelson, who also serves on the planning panel, said the project had not received required approval from Congress, nor had Congress appropriated any money for it. The plan submitted to the commission does not include a reference to military use cited by Trump and other administration officials, Mendelson said.
“We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plans,” he said.
Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.

“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans, as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.

Trump arch construction blocked after federal approval The Trump administration hoped to begin construction immediately after a federal panel approved its arch late Thursday. But just after midnight, the judge issued an order blocking work for 14 days.

Demonstrators stand at Memorial Circle to protest President Trump's proposed arch on Thursday night as a federal panel heard hours of testimony from concerned citizens. It voted to approve the structure. Tom Brenner/Getty Images hide caption
A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's arch, stopping work the administration had hoped to begin immediately.

Just before midnight Friday, District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan issued an order — finalized and made public minutes later - barring the government from any construction work for 14 days, granting a request filed days earlier by the governments of D.C. and Virginia .

She laid out her reasoning in a 33-page opinion , in which she scrutinized the administration's competing justifications for the arch — particularly its sudden emphasis on national security — and agreed that the local governments are likely to be harmed by its construction. The 250-foot arch would stand in Memorial Circle, a traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery.
Trump's arch is on the verge of federal approval. But a judge could block construction

Trump administration officials have said work would take place 20 hours a day, year-round, for two to three years. In addition to questioning the arch's legality, D.C. and Virginia argue the construction would cause all sorts of financial and logistical disruptions.
"The threatened harms will materialize as soon as construction begins, in part because the traffic disruptions will occur immediately," Chutkan agreed.

Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after a federal planning commission packed with presidential allies granted final approval to the arch in an 8-4 vote. The National Capital Planning Commission heard nearly eight hours of impassioned pleas from veterans, lawmakers, residents and concerned citizens opposed to the structure.
The Trump administration had previously told the court it could begin excavation work that same day, despite lacking authorization from Congress and an expanding legal challenge.

A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued the government earlier this year, arguing that an arch is unlawful without Congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. The Democratic governments of D.C. and Virginia jointly filed a similar lawsuit last weekend.
Chutkan consolidated the lawsuits and asked the government to notify the court within an hour of commission approval, setting the stage for an 11th-hour ruling.

Thursday started with a protest on Memorial Circle, where dozens of people spoke against the arch. The grass underfoot was already marked with white paint. Lawyers for the government told the court in a midday filing that the lines were painted on Saturday by its designated construction firm, seemingly without authorization from the National Park Service.
The commission meeting began at 1 p.m. It was held virtually because of the high volume of public testimony: 131 people were signed up to speak.

Just minutes into public testimony, the livestream crashed, lengthening the meeting by about an hour until it was restored. Over the course of nearly nine hours, commissioners heard from dozens of veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and concerned citizens from D.C. and beyond.
Trump aims to leave a physical legacy in D.C., bulldozing norms along the way

Among their many concerns , critics said the structure would obstruct an important view , insult service members buried on the hallowed ground of nearby Arlington National Cemetery and add a layer of risk to the notoriously complicated D.C. airspace. They have questions about its legality and its cost, which the administration has not confirmed.

The Democrats’ stunning midterm victory should broaden Australia’s alliance with the US, observers say, even as a new power base emerges in Washington, affecting Aukus, datacentre development and relations with China.

Cabinet ministers, diplomats and Australia’s defence industrial sector closely watched the results this week, with control of the US Congress flipping to the Democrats and the outlook for Donald Trump’s final two years in office badly dinted.
Bruce Wolpe on what Trump will do after the ‘profound result’ of the US midterms - podcast

Public fury over rising living costs, particularly fuel prices, and the impact of datacentres, were also two factors in the midterms results that carry warnings for the Australian government, analysts said.
Bruce Wolpe, a senior fellow at the United States Studies Centre, said Trump’s ability to rile up voters had been undermined by cost of living.
Wolpe said the Albanese government was taking a hit because of the economic fallout from the Iran war.
“I think a lot of people are wondering what does this [Australian] government do?” he said. “Have they lost control of the economy?
“In January, before the Iran war, the outlook looked pretty good. But now, after going through a budget process and the war … people are just very uncertain as to where this is going to end up.
“It is not an immediately solvable problem, and people really dislike it.”
Westpac’s head of international economics, Elliot Clarke, said the landslide midterms results had “dramatically changed” the outlook for the Iran war, which could affect the economy in Australia.
“It has changed the ‘atmospherics’ around the Middle East conflict,” he said. “It’s positive news.”
There was a steep drop in the global oil price as the election results filtered out. The Brent crude benchmark, which had threatened to pass its April peak, has instead plunged by 20%.
More confidence in a potential resolution in the Middle East would also help curb inflation and help central banks hold back on rate hikes, according to Clarke.
“It definitely changes the calculus,” he said.
Coalition frontbencher Andrew Hastie said the results showed economic messaging was critical.

“People feel worse off after tariffs and after the war in Iran, and Donald Trump has said a few times now that he doesn’t really care,” he told 2GB. “Our job is always to deliver better outcomes for the Australian people.”

Arthur Sinodinos, a former ambassador to Washington, said the change on Capitol Hill was a chance for Australian officials to progress policy goals with both US parties, and to consider the relationship beyond the 2028 presidential election.

summary_zh: 唐纳德·特朗普总统寻求将椭圆形办公室打造成国家纪念碑，以确保其设计不会“被愚蠢的人撕毁”
body_en: Trump signs proclamation to try to prevent changes to gold-covered Oval Office | Donald Trump
President seeks to make Oval Office a national monument to ensure designs are not ‘ripped down by stupid people’

Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces which he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.

In the days since his party suffered historic defeats in the midterm elections, the president has seemingly turned his attention to the many renovation projects he has begun across the nation’s capital. Sitting behind the Resolute Desk on Thursday, Trump declared the Oval Office a “national monument”.
“I’m going to be signing a document which will make them into a landmark for the ages,” he told reporters in the gold-covered Oval Office.

According to the president, the proclamation would ensure the West Wing rooms would not be “touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape”.
“I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come and take it down and try and do something with it,” he said.

“Every once in a while they’ll look and they’ll say, oh, maybe what we’ll do is we’ll put some glass up that’s a little bit better or something, and I say no, you’re not going to do anything. We’re going to leave this as it is,” he continued.
“If anyone ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you’ll call me wherever I may be, and I will come back here and I will make sure it never happens.”

Since returning to office, Trump has embarked on a series of White House “beautification” projects, most notably the demolition of the East Wing to make way for a $600m ballroom , as well the building of a permanent granite helipad on the South Lawn.

Speaking to reporters from the Oval Office, the president defended his wider renovation work at the White House, saying the building’s exterior had suffered from years of deterioration. He pointed to cracked windows, damaged stonework and broken decorative features, saying he had paid for repairs and hired skilled workers to restore them.
“When you looked at that wall one year ago, it was badly damaged from years of service,” he said, adding that exterior columns had also been in “horrible shape”.

On the desk next to where he signed the proclamation was a red baseball cap emblazoned with the word “Veto” – an explicit reminder of his threat to block the legislative priorities and bills passed by the new Democratic-controlled Congress next year.

Democrats made significant gains in several traditionally Republican states where Trump had previously won, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa, by campaigning on issues including affordability and tackling corruption, while also securing control of Congress.

Trump’s opulent redesign of the Oval Office has drawn criticism, including from former president Barack Obama, who recently joked that “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”
Obama’s remark prompted a coordinated response from the White House, with treasury secretary Scott Bessent appearing to hit back by dining at a Cheesecake Factory.

In a final appeal ahead of the midterm elections, Trump held a press conference highlighting the delayed results of his $14m renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, while blaming Joe Biden for the algae that had accumulated in its waters.
“This was in the Biden era … Look, it’s not an easy thing. The algae is brutal. It forms easily. All you saw was dirt and filth and paper and everything else for years,” Trump said on Monday.
Two days later, as the scale of his party’s staggering losses came into focus, Trump led a media tour of the White House Ballroom construction site, where he marveled at the renovations to come.
body_zh: 特朗普签署公告，试图阻止金色椭圆形办公室发生变化|唐纳德·特朗普
总统寻求将椭圆形办公室打造成国家纪念碑，以确保设计不会“被愚蠢的人撕毁”
唐纳德·特朗普周四签署了一份公告，表示将阻止未来的政府改变他对椭圆形办公室和内阁会议室的设计，他宣称这些空间是应该保护的国家古迹。
自从他的政党在中期选举中遭受历史性失败以来，总统似乎将注意力转向了他在首都开始的许多改造项目。周四，特朗普坐在坚决办公桌后面，宣布椭圆形办公室为“国家纪念碑”。
“我将签署一份文件，使它们成为千古的里程碑，”他在金色椭圆形办公室对记者说。
总统表示，该公告将确保西翼的房间不会“被任何人触碰、破坏、被愚蠢的人撕毁，以建造形状略有不同的东西”。
“我只是认为非常重要的是不允许任何人过来把它拆下来并尝试用它做点什么，”他说。
“每隔一段时间，他们就会看一下，然后说，哦，也许我们要做的就是加一些玻璃，这样会好一点或者什么，我说不，你什么也不做。我们将保持原样，”他继续说道。
“如果有人决定来开始拆除墙壁，无论我在哪里，你都会给我打电话，我会回到这里，我将确保它永远不会发生。”
自重返办公室以来，特朗普开始实施一系列白宫“美化”项目，其中最著名的是拆除东翼，为耗资6亿美元的宴会厅腾出空间，以及在南草坪修建永久性花岗岩直升机停机坪。
总统在椭圆形办公室向记者发表讲话，为他在白宫进行的更广泛的翻修工作进行了辩护，称该建筑的外观多年来一直在恶化。他指着破裂的窗户、损坏的石雕和破损的装饰，说他已经支付了维修费用，并聘请了熟练工人来修复它们。
“当你一年前看那堵墙时，你会发现它因多年的使用而受到严重损坏，”他说，并补充说外部柱子也“形状可怕”。
在他签署公告的地方旁边的桌子上有一顶红色棒球帽，上面印有“否决”一词——明确提醒人们，他威胁要阻止明年民主党控制的新国会通过的立法优先事项和法案。
民主党在特朗普之前获胜的几个传统共和党州取得了重大进展，包括德克萨斯州、堪萨斯州、南卡罗来纳州和爱荷华州，他们在负担能力和解决腐败等问题上进行了竞选活动，同时也确保了对国会的控制。
特朗普对椭圆形办公室的华丽重新设计引起了批评，其中包括前总统巴拉克·奥巴马(Barack Obama)，他最近开玩笑说“他让白宫看起来像萨达姆·侯赛因(Saddam Hussein)开了一家芝士蛋糕工厂。到处都是黄金。”
奥巴马的言论引发了白宫的协调反应，财政部长斯科特·贝森特似乎通过在芝士蛋糕工厂用餐来进行回击。
在中期选举前的最后呼吁中，特朗普举行了一场新闻发布会，强调了他耗资 1400 万美元翻修林肯纪念堂倒影池的延迟结果，同时将水域中藻类堆积的原因归咎于乔·拜登。
“那是在拜登时代……看，这不是一件容易的事。藻类很残酷。它很容易形成。多年来你看到的都是泥土、污物、纸张和其他一切，”特朗普周一表示。
两天后，随着共和党惊人损失的规模成为人们关注的焦点，特朗普带领媒体参观了白宫宴会厅建筑工地，他对那里即将进行的翻修工程感到惊叹。

summary: Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined. Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called by the AP.

body_en: Here are the House races left on the map : NPR

Here are the House races left on the map Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined. Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called by the AP.
Democrats are poised to have a strong majority in the upcoming Congress. The final numbers are still being determined and several races are still outstanding.

A few in California are being contested by two candidates in the same party. So it's clear which party will hold the seat, even if it's not clear who will win. Others are too close to call or there aren't enough ballots counted to know which candidate will prevail. In many places in the country, it takes a while to count votes . That's normal and expected.
Here's where things stand in the races that are waiting to be called in the House by The Associated Press

In the Senate, there are two races outstanding, Alaska and Mississippi. Because Alaska uses ranked choice voting and no candidate in the four-person race has achieved a 50% majority in the count, it may proceed to another round of counting later this month. Mississippi uses a more traditional electoral system but a large number of provisional ballots — called affidavit ballots in the state — are taking time to count. Less than 2,000 votes separate the top two candidates in that race.

title_en: Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine
title_zh: 梅拉尼娅·特朗普吹捧她在俄罗斯和乌克兰之间斡旋达成的罕见协议
summary: The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.
summary_zh: 俄罗斯占领的奥列什基市暂停六天之际，政府正加紧努力达成结束乌克兰战争的协议
body_en: Melania Trump touts rare agreement she brokered between Russia and Ukraine The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 05: First lady Melania Trump gives hand written letters to Russian special envoy and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund Kirill Dmitrievon (L) and Ukrainian human rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets (C) to deliver to their presidents during an event on a temporary Russia-Ukraine ceasefire at the White House on November 5, 2026 in Washington, DC. Samuel Corum/Getty Images hide caption
First lady Melania Trump hosted a rare meeting between Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House to recognize a temporary ceasefire in southeastern Ukraine .
The six-day pause from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky comes as the administration ramps up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.
"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the divisions of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace."

Trump has accomplished something that has so far eluded her husband - helping broker a temporary ceasefire and bringing together representatives of the two sides in acknowledgement of the human costs of the war.
The White House sees it as a diplomatic breakthrough, but some European analysts worry the efforts can backfire.
The temporary reprieve, which expired on Sunday, enabled humanitarian aid to reach the city while allowing hundreds of residents to be evacuated.
Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special envoy, thanked the first lady. He said Putin personally gave the instructions to ensure the successful implementation of the ceasefire.

"On behalf of President Putin, on behalf of the people of the Russian Federation, we would like to thank first lady Melania Trump for her distinguished humanitarian role in resolving a key situation and resolving this humanitarian issue," he said.
Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets presented Melania Trump with an award for her humanitarian work. The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, is Ukraine's highest award for women.
"I have only one request from all Ukrainian nation," Lubinets said, "please continue doing your wonderful work and support people."
The event comes just days before the U.S. leads a new round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.
President Trump also met with Dmitriev at the White House.
Trump told reporters that the sides were close to reaching a deal.

"It's going to be an agreement. It's going to be a big agreement, ‌and ⁠it's going to involve more than Ukraine," he said. "I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It's ⁠going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled."

Heather Conley, who worked on European issues in President George W. Bush's State Department, supports all efforts to help suffering Ukrainians, but she also said the U.S. must be careful not to normalize Russia's bad behavior.

华盛顿特区 - 11 月 5 日：第一夫人梅拉尼娅·特朗普于 2026 年 11 月 5 日在华盛顿特区白宫举行的俄罗斯-乌克兰临时停火活动期间，向俄罗斯特使兼俄罗斯直接投资基金负责人基里尔·德米特里冯（左）和乌克兰人权监察员德米特罗·鲁宾涅茨（中）递交了手写信，以便转交给两国总统。塞缪尔·科鲁姆/盖蒂图片社隐藏标题栏
第一夫人梅拉尼娅·特朗普在白宫主持了一次罕见的俄罗斯和乌克兰官员会面，承认乌克兰东南部的临时停火。
俄罗斯占领的奥列什基市暂停六天之际，美国政府正在加紧努力，以达成结束乌克兰战争的协议。
“我们选择了人性而不是战争，”第一夫人说。 “不可否认，无辜人民的生命必须超越战争的分歧。我希望奥列什基能够激发更大的和平。”
特朗普完成了她丈夫迄今为止未能完成的事情——帮助促成临时停火，并让双方代表聚集在一起，承认战争造成的人员伤亡。
白宫认为这是一次外交突破，但一些欧洲分析人士担心这些努力可能会适得其反。
周日到期的临时禁令使人道主义援助能够到达该市，同时使数百名居民得以疏散。
俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京的特使基里尔·德米特里耶夫向第一夫人表示感谢。他说，普京亲自作出指示，确保停火协议顺利实施。
他说：“我们谨代表普京总统，代表俄罗斯联邦人民，感谢第一夫人梅拉尼娅·特朗普在解决关键局势和这一人道主义问题方面所发挥的杰出人道主义作用。”
乌克兰人权监察员德米特罗·鲁比内茨向梅拉尼娅·特朗普颁发了人道主义工作奖。一级奥尔哈公主勋章是乌克兰授予女性的最高奖项。
鲁比涅茨说：“我只有一​​个来自乌克兰全国人民的请求，请继续做好你们出色的工作并支持人民。”
此次活动发生在美国下周在阿布扎比举行新一轮俄罗斯和乌克兰和平谈判的几天前。
特朗普总统还在白宫会见了德米特里耶夫。
特朗普告诉记者，双方即将达成协议。
“这将是一项协议。这将是一项重大协议，而且涉及的不仅仅是乌克兰，”他说。 “我什至可以说，这可能涉及整个欧洲。这将是一项重大而美好的协议，每个人都会感到兴奋。”
曾在乔治·W·布什总统的国务院负责欧洲问题的希瑟·康利支持一切帮助受苦受难的乌克兰人的努力，但她也表示，美国必须小心，不要让俄罗斯的不良行为正常化。

title_en: Mississippi Senate race still a toss-up, with razor-thin margin
title_zh: 密西西比州参议院竞选是颠簸的，利润率极低
summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
summary_zh: 深红色密西西比州的参议院竞选周三上午仍未解决，因为民主党人斯科特·科洛姆（ Scott Colom ）发起了一场令人惊讶的竞争挑战
body_en: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

With about 96% of the vote in, at one point Wednesday morning just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. By Friday morning, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by just over 1,800 votes.
State officials say several thousand ballots still need to be counted, and both campaigns have expressed confidence.

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state the President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said Wednesday there are approximately 3,600 outstanding mail ballots and an unknown number of affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, from voters whose eligibility needs to be confirmed. Absentee ballots must be received within five business days, while affidavit ballots must be processed within the 10-day window that counties have to certify results, which ends Nov. 13.
Mississippi does not allow recounts, so a winner will be decided based on a plurality of votes.
Both parties are keeping a close eye on the process. CBS News has confirmed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has deployed lawyers and resources to the state to monitor the count.
"I'm confident that ultimately Mississippi has decided to go in a new direction," Colom told reporters after greeting campaign volunteers Thursday morning in Jackson.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee and Hyde-Smith campaign filed a request for all counties to separate and preserve all affidavit ballots. The Colom campaign called the move a "desperate stunt." His counsel also sent a new letter to Mississippi's 82 counties asking them to respect election procedures.

Hyde-Smith predicted that she will win reelection, posting on X : "We believe thousands of votes remain to be counted from dozens of Republican counties, and we are confident those votes will reinforce her path to victory."

At a news conference Thursday, Mississippi Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst insisted the election "is far from being over" and noted the state party has attorneys and observers throughout the state to ensure all legally cast ballots are counted.

Then-President Joe Biden nominated Colom for a federal judgeship in the Northern District of Mississippi, but Hyde-Smith declined to back his nomination in April 2023, citing questions about Colom's stance on transgender issues and other concerns. Colom won the support of Mississippi's other Republican senator, Roger Wicker .

Under the Senate's "blue slip" tradition, the Senate Judiciary Committee generally does not move forward with federal district court nominees unless the senators who represent the judicial district sign off — preventing Colom from being confirmed to a lifetime judicial appointment. About two and a half years later, Colom launched his campaign for Senate.
Colom told CNN that "not having a federal judgeship is not a motivating factor for me at all" in his Senate campaign, saying he forgives Hyde-Smith.

The Mississippi contest is one of just two still-unresolved Senate races. Alaska's Senate race between GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

body_en: Wildlife advocates incensed as documents show state paid out $2,000 per kill in effort to shrink state’s wolf population

Idaho officials paid hunters thousands of dollars for killing a dozen newborn wolf pups this spring, including what appears to be at least one full litter killed in or near its den, according to state records shared with the Guardian and Public Domain.

The wolf pup killings have incensed wildlife advocates in Idaho, where state wildlife officials have been ordered to take extraordinary measures to shrink the state’s re-introduced wolf population amid complaints from the livestock industry and big game hunting outfitters.

A law passed five years ago by the Republican-dominated state legislature loosened restrictions on hunting seasons, removed restrictions on killing methods and allowed people to contract third parties to kill wolves. Individual hunters and trappers are able to buy an unlimited number of permits to kill wolves, which cost $14 each for state residents and $32 for non-residents.

In 2021, Idaho game officials also entered into an agreement with the Foundation for Wildlife Management, a non-profit devoted to reducing wolves to help boost deer and elk numbers, to reimburse expenses to any hunter and trapper who provides proof of killing a wolf. The program pays for a wide range of expenses, including truck payments, fuel, ammunition and outdoor clothing.

The reimbursement program paid $2,000 per wolf kill through the hunting season that ended in June, including the 12 pups, records from the state’s fish and game agency show. The program is funded with a mix of taxpayer money, hunting license sales and contributions from the Foundation for Wildlife Management. .

“It’s an abomination,” said Brooks Fahy, director of the advocacy group Predator Defense. “I think most people, even in Idaho, if they actually understood the depth of this, the fact that taxpayer dollars are paying for this – they would be appalled.”

“Let’s call this what it is – it’s a goddamned bounty,” Fahy said. “What kind of receipts are you going to show for 12 pups who weigh 12lbs? It’s ridiculous on its face and the state of Idaho should be ashamed.”
Neither the foundation nor the Idaho wolf depredation control board, a government entity that oversees payments for third-party wolf killings, responded to requests for comment.

Gray wolves were all but wiped off the map in the continental United States by the mid-20th century through government extermination programs , but the population has rebounded in Idaho since being reintroduced by the US Fish and Wildlife Service in 1995. That has reignited tensions with ranchers and big game outfitters whose livelihoods are affected by the animals.

Three separate hunters used rifles to kill a total of 12 wolf pups in Idaho’s northern panhandle region on April 25, the records show – though in at least two instances the records also include a contradictory statement saying that “no weapon” was used. The pups were likely between one and three weeks old by that date. Wolves give birth once a year in the spring.

Hunters and trappers must present a skull and hide with proof of sex attached to a wildlife officer for every wolf killed in the state. The officer normally takes a tooth sample, which allows state biologists to estimate the animal’s age and genetic information.
Officers did not take teeth samples from the 12 pups, however – likely because their teeth had yet to grow in or were too small to extract, according to Idaho fish and game biologist Cory Mosby.

Mosby confirmed that the 12 wolves documented in the records were pups. No state regulation bars the killing of pups, he said. Wildlife officials would normally restrict killing pups by closing the hunting and trapping seasons during the spring, when wolves typically give birth.

But the state management plan, adopted in 2023, mandates culling wolves to about 650 animals in spring, when wolf numbers typically peak. The state’s permissive hunting and trapping regulations, including the yearlong season, are designed to tamp wolf numbers down to that target and will likely become more restrictive as the population dwindles, Mosby said.

That day remains a long way away. Idaho wildlife authorities estimate that the population peaked at about 1,600 wolves in spring back in 2019. That figure for this year still stood at more than 1,100 wolves, despite aggressive hunting and trapping and state-backed payments to incentivize wolf killings. Mosby said that hitting the target would require consistently killing more than a third of the wolf population annually.

“They’re an incredibly impressive and resilient species,” Mosby said. “It takes sustained, high levels of harvest to get into what you call ‘additive’ mortality – where you’re actually removing animals.”
The records state that all 12 wolf pups were killed by “still stalk” – a method in which hunters spot an animal and then sneak up on it to take a shot.
But wolf experts said that the hunters responsible had more likely located the dens, monitored them until the mothers had given birth, then pulled the pups out to kill them.

title_en: Past White House adviser Raj Panjabi has written a playbook for 'living room' crises
title_zh: Past White House adviser Raj Panjabi has written a playbook for 'living room' crises
summary: Dr. Raj Panjabi is the author of Safer: A Playbook. His goal is to help people face a personal crisis — health, workplace, family conflicts — and "turn fear into action."
summary_zh: Dr. Raj Panjabi is the author of Safer: A Playbook. His goal is to help people face a personal crisis — health, workplace, family conflicts — and "turn fear into action."
body_en: Raj Panjabi knows a thing or two about living with uncertainty. His family fled Liberia during the civil war, coming to the U.S. when he was 9. And he and his wife faced a crisis when their youngest child was diagnosed with heart failure. A physician, he served as malaria coordinator and then as global health security adviser in the Biden White House during the pandemic. Ben de la Cruz/NPR hide caption
Dr. Raj Panjabi's new book has a simple title: Safer: A Playbook.
Yes, a playbook like the kind sports managers use to firm up a winning strategy. But playbooks aren't just for games.

"In the intensive care unit, we have a playbook when someone's heart stops beating," And when he was a White House health adviser during the COVID emergency, he says, "In the Situation Room, we had a playbook for pandemic preparedness."
Then there was his own family's situation — at age 1, his daughter was diagnosed with heart failure.
That experience inspired Panjabi to write a different kind of playbook. "I was frustrated that we didn't have a playbook for crises that appear in our own living room."

What he wrote is actually three books in one: The story of how he and his wife addressed their daughter's life-threatening condition; an exploration of public health issues that beset the globe – and straightforward advice for anyone with a living-room crisis. The book's chapter titles telegraph his philosophy: "Turn Denial Into Action." "Don't Go It Alone." "Get Ready to Pivot." "Embrace Uncertainty."

Panjabi was born to Indian parents in Liberia; his family immigrated to the United States when he was 9. He became a physician and went on to found the award-winning humanitarian group Last Mile Health, which employs community workers to bring health information to people in remote areas.
Raj Panjabi is interviewed at NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 30. Ben de la Cruz/NPR hide caption

We interviewed Raj Panjabi at NPR headquarters on October 30. He had just flown in from meetings in Boston, wearing a sharp-looking sports jacket he'd bought at the airport — because his mother, who sells men's clothing, is a tough critic of his fashion choices.

So one thing that happens in a crisis — and that a playbook can help address — is denial. You and your wife both dismissed early concerns about your daughter — thinking at first that her extremely low weight was because she was a picky eater.

I was wrought with the guilt of being a dad and missing this illness — and being a doctor and missing this illness in my own daughter. I thought it was a character flaw. What I learned is that it's not. Denial is the first stage of almost every crisis. It could be a medical emergency, like in the case of my daughter. It could be job loss, that layoff you never thought would affect you.
And what I learned in researching the book — it turns out we have a hard time detecting slow moving threats until they reach a tipping point.
Psychologists call it normalcy bias — the idea that tomorrow will look a lot like yesterday. Until, of course, it doesn't. The good news is that there are ways we can overcome that.
In the case of a slow-moving crisis like my daughter's illness, the very first thing you might do is set an if/then threshold. If I see a warning sign, I will act in X or Y way.
Your daughter is 9 now and has recovered. How do you deal with any lingering uncertainty about her heart health?

Every couple of years, she goes to the cardiologist and she gets an ultrasound of the heart. The trigger we're looking for is whether the heart's ability to squeeze is at a normal level or not. We'll see that well before we see any major heart failure. Allowing a trigger to do the monitoring for you allows you to feel some agency and allows you to control what you can control.

Health crises can be very personal — but also societal. In the United States, measles — eradicated 36 years ago, is back because parents are opting not to vaccinate their kids. What's the playbook for talking to those parents?
It's much easier to ask a blame-oriented question when someone's not protecting themselves or their community, such as "Why aren't you following the guidelines?"

body_en: How a ‘flaming liberal’ podcast host won a US House seat in conservative Missouri | US midterm elections 2026
Fred Wellman, host of the progressive podcast On Democracy, defeated longtime incumbent Republican Ann Wagner

F red Wellman’s victory in Missouri’s second congressional district on Tuesday was such a surprise that NBC News’s star data analyst Steve Kornacki didn’t even have a graphic prepared, he told supporters on election night.
Longtime Republican incumbent Ann Wagner, who had been widely expected to hold her seat, was swept aside as part of a broader wave of Democratic victories across the country.

Wellman, 61, had a lengthy career as an officer in the US army and later as a veterans advocate, but he is better known as an anti-Donald Trump, pro-democracy online media personality with more than 358,000 followers on X. (He met his fiancee on the social media platform, he said.)

He hosts a podcast called On Democracy for the progressive, anti-Trump MeidasTouch network, making him a non-traditional choice in a predominantly conservative state like Missouri. “Fred has always been a fighter and a powerful voice for the people when it matters most,” said MeidasTouch co-founder Ben Meiselas. “We’re incredibly proud of his success and thrilled to see him win.”
Wagner attempted to use Wellman’s media career against him, playing up his self-description as a “flaming liberal” several years ago on a podcast in a campaign advertisement.
While Wellman’s podcast, which he began four years ago, certainly raised his national media profile, he said he intentionally emphasized his local roots growing up in Kirkwood, Missouri.

“I didn’t want to be a national figure or national anti-Trump guy,” he said. “I wanted to be Fred from Kirkwood. And I think one of the reasons we won this race is because instead of trying to be this ‘famous person’ who’s running for his local office, I always said my job is to represent the people of Missouri. And I think that was a key strategy decision that I think paid off for us.”
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

No, I thought we would win. I was nervous, obviously. I thought it was 50/50. I believe a lot of folks were saying it was a toss-up. I was always worried about the amount of ads [Wagner] was able to run … But I knew from being present in the district and talking to people that we could do it, that we’ve created a bipartisan, a nonpartisan movement, that I had captured the coalition I needed to capture, which was all of labor came in with us, short of police and fire. And even the rank-and-file of the police and fire were backing me.
Why did you try to de-emphasize your national media and social media career when running for office?

I think it’s off-putting to people who are local. I think a lot of times it feels like they’re being used for your national ambitions, or that you want to be famous. I think especially for me, as being a social media person that was well known – somewhat, if you will – online, that people dismissed me as just looking for more clout. And I wanted to make it very clear: no, I was running to be a congressman representing 759,000 people of eastern Missouri. We were very focused on that. And then we showed it personally by being everywhere in the district and meeting people where they are, not relying solely on being internet famous. And I think that’s one of the reasons we did so well.
What did your family originally think of your decision to get into podcasting?

It’s a running joke that when I told my fiancee I wanted to start a podcast, she thought that was a terrible idea because it’s a little cliche being a middle-aged white guy with a podcast. But it was a great platform for me to tell my story – not my story, that’s the wrong way to put it – but to talk about democracy, talk about the threats to democracy, highlight some of the incredible voices: journalists, authors, politicians, thinkers. I’ve really enjoyed doing it. It’s been a great place. I’ve learned a lot. And the nice thing about doing it for so long – four years of doing a podcast – there are very few issues I hadn’t seen. So when it came time to be a congressman or a candidate, there’s very few things that hadn’t come across my radar at some point.
Did you think your candidacy caught Wagner off-guard?

Yes, absolutely. Well, we were considered safe even within the national movement. The Cook Political Report never moved us off as “safe Republican”. Never. I think the prognosticators felt that as a 34-year Republican seat, a 14-year incumbent who started out with $4.5m to my zero, and me not having that kind of wherewithal, they took the fact that the [Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee] and the other big national groups never came in, as a sign of weakness within my campaign … As we looked at the numbers and we looked at what was possible, I saw a real opportunity. I believed that Representative Wagner was much, much weaker than people realized. And I believed there was a chance, and I think my instincts proved out.
So, you’re heading to Washington DC on Sunday?

Orientation starts this Sunday. Got to figure out how to be a congressman. Congressman 101 … I’ve done public service. Same oath I swore as a 17-year-old, but obviously it’s a very different kind of service. Like I said, I’ve got 759,000 bosses now. I’ve got to answer to people who may not agree with me, who didn’t vote for me. And I owe them as good as I can do, and I owe them to be transparent as much as I can be and I owe them to be honorable.

title_en: The midterms blew open the 2028 map. Republicans are panicking.
title_zh: The midterms blew open the 2028 map. Republicans are panicking.
summary: Strategists on both sides agree: Ohio, Texas and Iowa should be competitive in 2028.
summary_zh: Strategists on both sides agree: Ohio, Texas and Iowa should be competitive in 2028.
body_en: Brutal red-state losses are raising alarm among Republicans about the 2028 presidential battlefield.

Democrats’ midterm blowout is upending the political calculus for future presidential campaigns, more than a dozen strategists on both sides told POLITICO. Republicans are stressing the ramifications of a major tranche of once-reliably Republican Electoral College votes being in jeopardy, while Democrats are weighing how much surprise wins on red turf should reshape their electoral strategy.
“Last night undoubtedly made the mechanics of winning in 2028 harder for Republicans,” said former Trump 2020 campaign manager Bill Stepien.

Stepien lamented that Republicans had lost both once-swing Midwestern states like Ohio that Trump had brought toward the GOP, as well as formerly red Sunbelt states like Georgia and Arizona that have moved steadily left in the Trump era.
" Waging a campaign for president in Texas is big, expensive, and not something Republicans have had to do for a long time,” he added. “The impacts of last night are real."

Trump had rearranged the electoral map for the past 12 years with a blue-collar coalition that moved Ohio and Iowa safely into Republicans’ ledger, turned Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania into true swing states and did enough in the Sun Belt to keep Texas from being in play. But that all fell apart this week as Democrats romped across the map. If things don’t change fast after Tuesday’s results, Republicans fear that the party’s next nominee will confront a bleak map akin to 2008 or 2012, when the GOP had an excruciatingly narrow path to victory.

Marc Short, who served as chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence, compared this year’s GOP gutting to Republicans’ 2006 midterm shellacking, which foreshadowed Democrats taking the White House and building massive majorities two years later.
“[Republicans] didn’t bottom in 2006, you bottomed after 2008,” said Short.

Democrats know that recreating their historically large estimated 14-point national popular vote blowout isn’t likely in the 2028 presidential election, and that Trump’s historic unpopularity was a major factor in the midterms.

“It’s not fait accompli that any of those voters that came over will stay with us, in the same way that they didn't stay with Donald Trump after this last cycle, or they didn't stay with Joe Biden after 2020,” said Dan Kanninen, former battleground states director for former Vice President Kamala Harris’ 2024 campaign. But the electoral map suddenly looks a lot different to strategists than it did a few days ago.
"In this environment, every state eventually becomes a swing state,” said Antjuan Seawright, a South Carolina-based Democratic strategist who advised Hakeem Jeffries this cycle.

Democrats are particularly excited about their breakthrough in Texas, which — like Arizona and Georgia before it — has been trending to the left for years, driven by demographic change and suburban voters’ realignment. The state’s rapid Hispanic growth meant the swing in Hispanic voters back toward Democrats pushed the state especially hard towards them this cycle. “If we weren't already considering Texas a swing state in 2028, we are now,” said Melissa Morales, the executive director of SOMOS PAC, a Latino voter engagement group.
Democrats swept Texas’ statewide offices on Tuesday despite being massively outspent, with Sen.-elect James Talarico leading the way with a 12-point blowout victory.
Talarico told POLITICO after his win that Texas is “absolutely” on the presidential map for 2028, and said he would “urge every 2028 candidate to vigorously compete in our state.”

Some Democrats urged party leaders to press their organizing advantage in Texas, seeing the state’s Black and Latino voters as central to the future of the party in a state where the Republican machine had helped keep the state out of reach for Democrats.

Republican collapses in Ohio and Iowa, two longtime swing states that President Obama carried twice that had moved hard right under Trump, have panicked some GOP strategists in those states. Democrats won Senate and governor’s races in both states Tuesday, as well as flipping a half-dozen House seats between them as they romped across the region. Republicans in both states warn that the era of GOP dominance might have been more closely tied to Trump’s unique populist appeal and could be competitive in two years — an appeal that has taken a major hit since he returned to the White House.

“You lived off Trump’s brand, and Trump’s brand did a lot of good for the state of Iowa. We won a lot of things here. But you can also die by the brand as well,” said Bob Vander Plaats, an influential evangelical leader in Iowa.
In Ohio, ancestrally Democratic blue-collar areas rebounded hard back to the left.

“Ohio should be considered a battleground,” Ohio GOP strategist Curt Steiner said. Republicans see the massive losses in all the future presidential battlegrounds as a huge blow to their organizational infrastructure in those states. Stepien said he would regularly lean on GOP governors in battleground states for guidance and strategy while helming Trump’s 2020 campaign, which he called a “massive advantage.” “You're going to save time, you're going to save money, you're going to have to put less staff into the state. You're going to have more local know-how,” Stepien said. “It is an automatic advantage to be able to tap into something that's existing and that's been tested.”
After Tuesday’s victories, Democrats hold the governor’s seats in all 10 presidential battleground states.

title_en: Low birth rates were emptying public schools. ICE deportations are now making it worse
title_zh: Low birth rates were emptying public schools. ICE deportations are now making it worse
summary: School enrollment was already expected to plunge by 2 million kids by 2030. Education experts say deporting immigrant families, many with school-age children, is making the crisis worse.
summary_zh: School enrollment was already expected to plunge by 2 million kids by 2030. Education experts say deporting immigrant families, many with school-age children, is making the crisis worse.
body_en: Low birth rates were emptying public schools. ICE deportations are now making it worse School enrollment was already expected to plunge by 2 million kids by 2030. Education experts say deporting immigrant families, many with school-age children, is making the crisis worse.

Kelly Gonez, a longtime school board member in the Los Angeles Unified School District, says public school enrollment declines worsened after ICE raids escalated in the city in 2025. District officials say low birth rates and the loss of immigrant children in classrooms mean school campuses will likely have to close. Carlos Jaramillo for NPR hide caption

LOS ANGELES — Long before the Trump administration started deporting hundreds of thousands of immigrants, many with school-age children, public schools nationwide faced a massive and accelerating drop in student enrollment caused mostly by shrinking families.

"Birth rates here in Los Angeles County have been declining for decades, which means fewer children enrolled in our schools," said Kelly Gonez, a board member in the LA Unified School District (LAUSD), the second largest in the country, which lost more than 300,000 students over the last two decades.
LA isn't alone. The population of children under age 18 began to fall nationwide after 2010, according to U.S. Census data , dropping by roughly 2.1 million kids through 2025 .

With public schools in much of the country facing a demographic cliff, the Trump administration last year began detaining and expelling large numbers of foreign residents. A study by the Migration Policy Institute found as many as 1.9 million people left the U.S. during the first 18 months of Trump's second term.

As part of the crackdown effort, federal officials weakened restrictions that prevented ICE agents from operating near public schools. "Many of our families immediately went into hiding," Gonez said. "We were predicting a 2% drop in enrollment. It was double that."

Researchers who study education and population trends aren't surprised. This is the first time in nearly a century, since the era of the Great Depression, that birth rates and immigration levels are low at the same time. Large-scale deportations mean even bigger and more rapid changes in areas with large immigrant communities.

"The U.S. isn't alone in facing the challenges of demographic decline," said Thomas Dee, an economist who specializes in education policy at Stanford University. "To stop or slow immigration really exacerbates those problems. Communities are now confronting very painful decisions about closing schools."

Special needs teacher Deja Nebula sets up an art installation displaying names and faces of people who have been detained or deported during ICE raids in Southern California, at Olvera Street Plaza in Los Angeles, July 2025. Damian Dovarganes/AP hide caption

The scale of decline is daunting. According to the U.S Department of Education , the number of kids in public schools nationwide peaked in 2019 and fell by roughly 1.5 million students as of the 2024 school year.

Based on data gathered before Trump's immigration crackdown began, federal researchers project enrollment will decline by at least another 2 million students by 2030. That would mean a 7% national decline in roughly a decade.
40 states see public school enrollment declines
An empty classroom is seen at Hollywood High School in L.A. The school district has begun a process aimed at closing and consolidating schools. Rodin Eckenroth/Getty Images hide caption

It's unclear how large or sustained the impact of Trump-era immigration policies will be on enrollment trends. Dee and other researchers say that depends on how long ICE crackdowns and other restrictions remain in place.

In the short term, the blow to many districts could be severe. When Dee studied public schools in communities hit by ICE raids in California's Central Valley in 2025, he found student daily absences spiked more than 20% .

Texas, meanwhile, saw the number of kids in classrooms plunge statewide last year by more than 76,000 students. The vast majority of that drop came among Hispanic kids and the children of immigrant families, according to a study by the Texas Education Agency .

Florida, home to a large community of Haitian refugees who were stripped of temporary protected status by the Trump administration in July, saw a big drop in enrollment this year. The state's two largest public school districts, Miami-Dade and Broward County , lost roughly 30,000 children combined in a single year.

title_en: Poll: Republicans and Democrats can agree on one thing. They’re divided.
title_zh: Poll: Republicans and Democrats can agree on one thing. They’re divided.
summary: POLITICO’s polling before Election Day showed that both parties would be left without clear direction amid a blue wave. And then the blue wave hit.
summary_zh: POLITICO’s polling before Election Day showed that both parties would be left without clear direction amid a blue wave. And then the blue wave hit.
body_en: Tuesday’s blue wave didn’t resolve either party’s internal divides. In fact, The POLITICO Poll shows they may even get worse.

Even ahead of Election Day, Republicans were already torn over how much to blame President Donald Trump for the scale of the defeat, weeks of polling show. While Trump distances himself from the electoral blowout — saying the loss was because he wasn’t on the ballot himself — some Republicans are beginning to weigh what a post-Trump GOP looks like.

Democrats, on the other hand, have scored a large-enough victory that instead of being united, nearly all factions of the party can claim it as evidence of support for their agenda, according to the surveys conducted by PF Global. Tuesday’s decisive wave, therefore, has done little to move them past the moderate and progressive infighting that has shaped much of this cycle.
One thing is clear: Both party’s leaders have a lot of work to do to stitch together a winning coalition ahead of a critical 2028 presidential race.

Here are some key takeaways from what voters were telling us right before they delivered a historically heavy blow to the president. (We’re polling them again soon to see how they may have shifted in the wake of the election.)
Republicans voters were torn over whether the midterms would divide their party

Before the elections, Republican midterm voters told The POLITICO Poll they were confident about a victory in the House and the Senate. Despite that, 29% felt that the GOP would come out of the elections more divided, while another 29% said it would come out more unified.
That’s compared with 45% of Democratic voters who said they expected more unity in their party after the election results — even before they knew what would happen.

Republican strategists and lawmakers have already issued stark warnings about the future of the GOP if the party doesn’t learn from voters’ frustrations with the economy, the Iran war and the Trump administration.

“Tonight’s shellacking should be a wake-up call,” Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) wrote in a lengthy Substack post on Tuesday night. “But if our response is to blame the media, the polls, or the voters, we’ll have learned absolutely nothing. We might start by looking in the mirror."
Trump’s coalition shattered — and many of his voters want to distance from him

Some Republicans are directly blaming Trump, who saw his coalition shatter on Tuesday night. The blue wave spared no region : Red counties and blue counties, Hispanic-heavy counties and white counties, urban areas and suburban areas all shifted to the left.
The POLITICO Poll shows there’s been a critical split between Trump voters who identify as MAGA — his most loyal supporters — and those who don’t, who make up the softer part of his 2024 coalition.

A majority of MAGA Trump voters said they would see a midterm election loss as a reason to move closer to Trump’s agenda. Non-MAGA Trump voters said the opposite: For them, a defeat in the House and the Senate was a reason to break away.

The fracture will persist beyond the election results — and it reflects the fact that Republicans’ voter base has been falling apart on a number of issues over the course of the last year. The POLITICO Poll has repeatedly shown that non-MAGA Trump voters break away from their MAGA bedfellows on everything from affordability to ICE to the war in Iran to data centers.

“It’s time to consider what life is going to be like after Donald Trump,” said Jonathan Fletcher, register of deeds and former GOP chair of Gaston County, North Carolina, where failed Senate nominee Michael Whatley’s watch party was held. “Trump has done some excellent things, and I appreciate that, but it can't be the party of Trump forever.”
Democrats are not on the same page about what major wins mean for party direction

The Democratic Party needs to brace for some fiery discussions of its own. Our polling showed that the scale of the victory would shape the direction Democratic voters would want to see from the party.
A plurality of Democratic midterm voters said a massive victory Tuesday would be a reason to run progressive candidates.

But that was driven by self-identified progressives, 61% of whom take that position. Moderate Democrats were more torn, with 35% saying the party should run more progressives in that scenario, and 36% saying the party should run moderates.

body_en: Bills have soared in rural state buffeted by tariffs and war in Iran – and Democrat Adam Hamilton’s stunning upset shows how deep economic frustrations run

L inda Olson always does her homework before voting – a trait she inherited from a family invested, and interested, in politics. Her father was a photographer who took portraits of political leaders in Washington, while her grandparents were farmers who cared deeply about their industry.

In 2024, Olson’s research led her to Donald Trump . She trusted that the then-former president would improve their economic realities in Junction City, Kansas – where she was born and raised – if he returned to the White House.

But two years later, life is just more expensive. Last winter, Olson was forced to spend $700 on medication while in between insurance plans, and skipped out on doses to stretch it out longer. Her grocery bills are unrecognizably high. And fuel prices are about a dollar per gallon more expensive than last year.
“I thought at the time that he was the better choice of what we had,” Olson said of Trump in 2024. Instead, he had been acting to “make himself richer instead of really helping the people”.

With frustrations like these looming large across the state, Kansans this week elected a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in nearly a century. It was a stunning upset in what was, until recently, thought to be a reliably red stronghold.
“I’ve seen what Roger Marshall did over the eight years or so that he’s been doing this,” said Olson, of the defeated Republican senator. “And I thought, it’s time we get fresh blood up there.”

Hamilton won, in part, by flipping six counties that backed Trump in 2024 and Marshall in 2020 – a sign that, even in more remote, and traditionally conservative, areas, patience with Trump and the Republican party is wearing thin.

“Not everybody that voted for Trump is part of this cult of personality that Trump has tried to make the Republican party into,” said Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, located in one of those six flipped counties.
“There are certainly people in Kansas that are like that: they’re pretty conservative, but they’re not beholden to Trump. And so I think one of the things this election did is peel off those people.”

M ost of Kansas is made up of farmland, encompassing nearly 45m acres and employing nearly one in five Kansans. Pastures, dotted with grazing cows and their calves, hug the state’s highways. Junction City is surrounded by its famed toffee-colored prairies, so expansive that untouched grassland stretches out to the horizon on both sides of the interstate.

Kansans who ranch and farm here, in the most rural corners of the state, remain deeply Republican, according to Smith. But neighboring communities such as Junction City and Emporia, where he teaches, depend heavily on the agricultural economy and have felt the impact of the strains on farmers.
“The people that live here aren’t actually farmers,” he said. “And they’re more likely to swing over to the other party because the economy is really taking a beating.”
David Aguirre, a 25-year-old who was born and raised in Junction City, and works at a Mexican restaurant, El Patron Dos, said that when the rest of the county is suffering, so does his work.
“It has, like, a domino effect for families,” he said. “If they’re not doing their best, they’re not gonna come out to eat, and then that affects staff, and cooks, and so on.”

While grocery shopping on Wednesday afternoon, Janet Grimm, who considers herself an independent, lamented her rising bills. Everything she picked out from the aisles was tagged with a red and yellow “sale” sticker, a conscious choice she needs to make now.
Kansas Democrat’s pitch to voters amid historic Senate bid: ‘I’m gonna just fight like hell’

Checking out with just a handful of items – eggs, chicken, some deli meat, two cucumbers and powdered sugar for the banana bread she was planning on making later that day – her total rang up to over $60.
Grimm voted for Hamilton, and felt hopefully that he would be able to improve the economy for people like her. “I really have faith that they’re going to do good,” she said.
body_zh: 受到关税和伊朗战争打击的农村州的账单飙升——民主党人亚当·汉密尔顿的令人震惊的不满表明了经济挫败感有多么严重
琳达·奥尔森（Linda Olson）总是在投票前做功课——这是她从一个对政治投资和感兴趣的家庭继承的特质。她的父亲是一位摄影师，为华盛顿的政治领导人拍摄肖像，而她的祖父母是农民，非常关心他们的行业。
2024 年，奥尔森的研究让她找到了唐纳德·特朗普。她相信，如果这位时任前总统回到白宫，他将改善她出生和长大的堪萨斯州章克申城的经济现实。
但两年后，生活变得更加昂贵。去年冬天，奥尔森在保险计划期间被迫花费 700 美元购买药物，并且为了延长服药时间而跳过了服药。她的杂货账单高得难以想象。燃油价格比去年每加仑贵一美元左右。
奥尔森在谈到 2024 年的特朗普时说：“我当时认为他是我们所拥有的更好的选择。”相反，他一直在“让自己变得更富有，而不是真正帮助人民”。
由于类似的挫败感在全州范围内日益凸显，堪萨斯州本周选举民主党人亚当·汉密尔顿进入美国参议院，这是近一个世纪以来的首次。对于直到最近还被认为是可靠的红色据点的地方来说，这是一个令人震惊的意外。
“我看到了罗杰·马歇尔在过去八年左右的时间里所做的事情，他一直在这样做，”奥尔森在谈到这位落败的共和党参议员时说道。 “我想，是时候我们为那里注入新鲜血液了。”
汉密尔顿获胜的部分原因是在 2024 年推翻了支持特朗普的六个县，在 2020 年推翻了支持马歇尔的六个县——这表明，即使在更偏远、传统上保守的地区，人们对特朗普和共和党的耐心也在逐渐减弱。
位于这六个翻转县之一的恩波里亚州立大学政治学教授迈克尔·史密斯说：“并不是所有投票给特朗普的人都是特朗普试图让共和党陷入这种个人崇拜的一部分。”
“堪萨斯州肯定有人是这样的：他们相当保守，但他们并不受制于特朗普。所以我认为这次选举所做的事情之一就是剥离了这些人。”
堪萨斯州大部分地区都是农田，占地近 4500 万英亩，雇用了近五分之一的堪萨斯人。牧场紧邻该州的高速公路，牧场上点缀着正在吃草的奶牛和它们的小牛。章克申城周围环绕着著名的太妃糖色大草原，其广阔无垠的草原一直延伸到州际公路两侧的地平线。
史密斯表示，在该州最农村的角落里放牧和务农的堪萨斯人仍然是坚定的共和党人。但他任教的章克申城和恩波里亚等邻近社区严重依赖农业经济，并感受到了农民承受压力的影响。
“住在这里的人实际上并不是农民，”他说。 “而且他们更有可能转向另一方，因为经济确实受到了打击。”
25 岁的戴维·阿吉雷 (David Aguirre) 在章克申城出生和长大，在一家墨西哥餐厅 El Patron Dos 工作，他说，当全县其他人都在受苦时，他的工作也是如此。
“这对家庭来说就像多米诺骨牌效应，”他说。 “如果他们没有尽力而为，他们就不会出来吃饭，这就会影响员工、厨师等。”
周三下午，在杂货店购物时，自认为是独立人士的珍妮特·格林 (Janet Grimm) 对自己不断上涨的账单感到遗憾。她从过道上挑选的所有东西都贴有红色和黄色的“促销”标签，这是她现在需要做出的有意识的选择。
堪萨斯州民主党在历史性的参议院竞选中向选民宣传：“我要拼命战斗”
只检查了几样东西——鸡蛋、鸡肉、一些熟食肉、两根黄瓜和她计划当天晚些时候制作香蕉面包的糖粉——她的总价就超过了 60 美元。
格林投票给了汉密尔顿，并希望他能够为像她这样的人改善经济。 “我真的相信他们会做好事，”她说。
