title_en: Alabama, Florida and Indiana carry out executions on same day
title_zh: 阿拉巴马州、佛罗里达州和印第安纳州在同一天执行死刑
summary: Unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day previously happened in 2010 Alabama, Florida and Indiana all carried out executions on Thursday in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same
summary_zh: 2010年阿拉巴马州、佛罗里达州和印第安纳州曾发生过三个州同时执行死刑的不寻常事件
body_en: Unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day previously happened in 2010
Alabama, Florida and Indiana all carried out executions on Thursday in an unusual instance of three states administering the death penalty on the same day.

In a record-tying 19th execution of the year, Florida executed Jesse Guardado via a three-drug lethal injection. Guardado had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton county home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing.
Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a house fire in 2010. And in Alabama, a man died by injection Thursday evening for his conviction in a fatal home robbery.

The death penalty in the US has faced renewed scrutiny since the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions after she survived two massive doses of pentobarbital.

Thursday’s executions were taking place the same day California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced he would commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying that he believed “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values”.
Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?

Newsom’s announcement was a sharp contrast with Florida, where outgoing Republican governor Ron DeSantis has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. His state has carried out more than half of the 34 executions so far this year in the US.
It is the second time since August that three states were set to carry out executions on a single day, although it remains unusual. Prior to this year, the last time it happened was 2010.
In Indiana on Thursday, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12.45am at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the state’s department of correction.

She said he had no final words. He had acknowledged killing his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped that governor Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined.
In Alabama, Michael Taylor died by lethal injection. In 1991, when he was 19, he beat two people, aged 83 and 79, to death with a metal bar during a robbery in their home in Gadsden.
Death penalty opponents had urged Alabama’s Republican governor, Kay Ivey, to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, but she declined.

Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty said: “If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life whom it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today.”

The state went forward with plans to execute Taylor, 54, by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

Alabama executed murderer Kenneth Smith in 2024 by nitrogen asphyxiation, in an episode that witnesses found excruciating, after previously failing to succeed in its attempt to kill him using lethal injection.
‘I’m not ready, brother’: US man to be put to death months after botched execution attempt

Meanwhile, in Indiana earlier on Thursday, lawyers failed to persuade the state governor to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans to assess a history of head injuries and mental health problems. They had asked for a life sentence.

Weisheit’s last objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week in front of the Indiana pharmacy board, the state regulatory agency.
body_zh: 2010年曾发生过三个州同一天执行死刑的罕见事件
周四，阿拉巴马州、佛罗里达州和印第安纳州均执行了死刑，这是三个州在同一天执行死刑的不同寻常的例子。
在今年创纪录的第 19 起处决中，佛罗里达州通过三种药物注射死刑处决了杰西·瓜尔达多 (Jesse Guardado)。瓜尔达多承认自己于 2004 年在沃尔顿县的家中刺死了一名 75 岁的妇女，然后偷走了她的珠宝盒、80 美元和其他贵重物品来购买毒品。这位女士帮助他找到了工作和住房。
几个小时前，印第安纳州处决了一名在 2010 年房屋火灾中杀死两名儿童的男子。在阿拉巴马州，周四晚间，一名男子因犯有致命的入室抢劫罪被注射死亡。
自从9月份田纳西州克里斯塔·派克(Christa Pike)处决失败以来，美国的死刑面临着新的审查，尽管在她两次服用大量戊巴比妥后幸存下来，法院拒绝了停止其他处决的努力。
周四执行死刑的同一天，加州州长加文·纽瑟姆 (Gavin Newsom) 宣布，他将对该州所有 548 名死刑犯进行减刑，并表示他认为“国家批准的杀戮与加州的价值观不相容”。
美国死刑数量激增——但在克里斯塔·派克被处决失败后，死刑的未来是什么？
纽瑟姆的声明与佛罗里达州形成鲜明对比，佛罗里达州即将卸任的共和党州长罗恩·德桑蒂斯像其他州长一样积极使用死刑。今年迄今为止，美国执行了 34 起处决，其中一半以上是由他所在的州执行的。
这是自八月以来第二次三个州在一天内执行死刑，尽管这仍然不寻常。今年之前，上一次发生这种情况是在2010年。
印第安纳州惩教部门发言人诺埃尔·拉塞尔 (Noelle Russell) 表示，周四上午 12 点 45 分，50 岁的杰弗里·威谢特 (Jeffrey Weisheit) 在印第安纳州密歇根城的州立监狱被宣布死亡。
她说他没有最后的话。他承认2010年在埃文斯维尔地区的一场房屋火灾中杀死了女友的两个孩子，但他希望州长迈克·布劳恩能够宽大处理，将他的刑期改为终身监禁。布劳恩拒绝了。
在阿拉巴马州，迈克尔·泰勒被注射死刑。 1991年，19岁的他在加兹登的家中遭遇抢劫，用金属棒将两名年龄分别为83岁和79岁的人打死。
死刑反对者曾敦促阿拉巴马州共和党州长凯·艾维将泰勒的刑期减至终身监​​禁，但她拒绝了。
废除死刑希望计划的埃丝特·布朗说：“如果国家杀死了迈克尔，那么杀死他的并不是那个犯下一生中最严重错误的19岁年轻人。而是今天坐在牢房里的那个成熟、受人尊敬、敬畏上帝的人。”
The state went forward with plans to execute Taylor, 54, by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional.他的律师反对在最后一刻改用注射死刑，因为他几年前选择了氮气作为死刑方法，但法官做出了对泰勒不利的裁决。
阿拉巴马州于 2024 年用氮气窒息法处决了凶手肯尼思·史密斯，这一事件令目击者感到十分痛苦，此前该州曾尝试使用注射死刑，但未能成功。
“我还没准备好，兄弟”：美国男子在处决失败数月后将被处决
与此同时，周四早些时候在印第安纳州，律师未能说服州长允许威谢特接受脑部扫描，以评估头部受伤史和心理健康问题。他们要求判处无期徒刑。
威谢特的最后一个反对意见集中在该州计划使用从一家药房购买的致命药物，该药房下周将在印第安纳州药房委员会（州监管机构）面前举行纪律听证会。

title_en: Case pitting "ER" against "The Pitt" can proceed, appeals court says
title_zh: Case pitting "ER" against "The Pitt" can proceed, appeals court says
summary: A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.
summary_zh: A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.
body_en: 'ER' and 'The Pitt' are similar enough for suit to proceed, appeals court finds - CBS News

Los Angeles — A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.

A three-judge panel from California's 2nd District Court of Appeal ruled unanimously on Wednesday that the trial court judge was correct to reject a motion to throw out the case from "The Pitt" production company Warner Bros. Television, which also produced "ER." But the judges dismissed Noah Wyle - the star of both shows and a producer on "The Pitt" - as a defendant along with two other producers who worked on both series.
The lawsuit is a clash between the makers of multiple Emmy-winning TV series that were each among the most important and acclaimed shows of their eras.

Crichton, the author of "Jurassic Park" and many other novels that became hit movies and TV shows, wrote the pilot script for "ER," the NBC show about a Chicago emergency room that redefined the medical drama genre and drew tens of millions of weekly viewers in its run from 1994 to 2009.

The lawsuit brought by Sherri Crichton was filed two years ago, before a single episode of "The Pitt" had aired. The HBO Max series that shows a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department has since become perhaps the most lauded series in television, winning two Emmys for best drama for its first two seasons and two best actor Emmys for Wyle.

Warner Bros. Television and CBS News have the same parent company following last month's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by the parent of CBS News, which was known at the time as Paramount Skydance and is now called Skydance.

Along with more technical legal issues, the judges had to decide whether the shows had at least the minimal similarity that would give the lawsuit enough merit to move forward. Their decision applies only to this early legal challenge and they did not rule on whether the plaintiffs had proved the "The Pitt" is derivative of "ER."

The court agreed with the plaintiff that "both shows provide commentaries on the healthcare system; they focus specifically on the emergency room and the difficult conditions under which the medical staff operates. Both shows take place, with little exception, in the emergency room, as opposed to other medical shows which track patients as they move out of the emergency room, or indeed never enter it."

The opinion also said that both feature "very fast pacing, and reactions to multiple overlapping crises. The fast-paced dialogue is (to a layperson) frequently incomprehensible shorthand and jargon, lending an air of immediacy and accuracy."

Warner Bros. Television said in a statement that "WBTV continues to maintain that 'The Pitt' is an entirely original series and that the claims against it are without merit. Nothing in the Court of Appeal's decision establishes otherwise, and WBTV looks forward to defending its position as the case proceeds."
The defendants argued in legal filings that the shows have "generic similarities" that would exist in "any dramatic story" that features "overworked doctors and staff."

The panel also unanimously dismissed as defendants Wyle, John Wells, who created "The Pitt" and worked on "ER," and R. Scott Gemmill, a "Pitt" executive producer who also worked on both shows. The judges found there was no evidence the three men knew the provisions of the Crichton contract that the lawsuit alleges they interfered with.
Sherri Crichton's lawsuit alleges "The Pitt" is a rebranded version of an unauthorized "ER" reboot that she had rejected.

Her husband had secured a coveted "frozen rights" provision in his contract for the series, prohibiting Warner Bros. from proceeding with any sequels, remakes, spinoffs or other productions derived from "ER" without Crichton's consent, or his estate's consent after his death from cancer in 2008.

After the production company could not reach an agreement with Sherri Crichton over a proposed "ER" reboot, the TV studio proceeded to develop and produce a series based on the same premise without permission, the lawsuit alleges.

The Associated Press has called five U.S. House races in North Carolina for Democrats, all of them in districts drawn to favor Republican candidates.
Of those districts, four are flipping from Republican control.

As of Thursday, the AP had called nine of the state's 14 House seats for Democrats and none for Republicans. It's a startling result for a delegation that went into Tuesday with 10 Republicans and four Democrats.
Here are North Carolina's 2026 election results
Races called Thursday that flipped from Republican to Democratic control included
High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson over first-term incumbent Rep. Addison McDowell in the Triad's 6th Congressional District.
Former West Virginia State Senator Richard Ojeda over National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Rep. Richard Hudson in the 9th Congressional District.
Paul Barringer over first-term incumbent Rep. Brad Knott in the 13th Congressional District, which wraps around the Raleigh exurbs.
LaKesha Womack over first-term incumbent Rep. Tim Moore, who previously served as speaker of the N.C. House of Representatives, in the 14th Congressional District.

North Carolina's Congressional map was redrawn in 2023 to significantly favor Republican candidates, and these four districts performed that way in 2024. The 14th District was the closest in that election, with Moore winning by about 16%, while the 6th District was the least competitive, with McDowell winning by more than 38%.
One of the candidates vying to replace Hudson as NRCC chair is U.S. Rep. Brian Jack, a Georgia Republican.

He wrote in a letter to fellow House Republicans that fellow GOP lawmakers may have contributed to the challenging environment. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, won the race for North Carolina's open U.S. Senate seat by nearly 20%.
What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina
"When Senate Republicans withdrew support from North Carolina weeks ago, they created a cascade that likely swept away many of our colleagues from that state," Jack wrote.
The AP also called northeastern North Carolina's 1st Congressional District for incumbent Democrat Rep. Don Davis on Thursday.

That's a district legislative Republicans redrew last year in an effort to make it easier for GOP candidates to win there, pulling Republican-leaning counties from the state's 3rd Congressional District to do so.

How criminals are racing to launder stolen crypto
The origin of fear around the adjustable-rate mortgage

What to know: North Korea just loves stealing crypto. They love it! It's become a major part of their economy. Last week, a state-sponsored hacking group called "TraderTraitor" executed the largest crypto theft in history, stealing $6.43 billion from Binance, a massive cryptocurrency exchange. $2.85 billion has been frozen or seized, according to Elliptic , a crypto analytics & compliance firm. But $3.35 billion is still linked to the group. "TraderTraitor" is actively trying to launder this money (yes, crypto is surprisingly traceable). A huge part of the stolen funds are in stablecoin, which can be frozen. Whatever isn't already frozen, the hacking group is trying to launder it and FAST. So how are they doing it?

How are the criminals laundering these assets?: Laundering this much crypto is NOT simple. The intelligence firm Elliptic broke down how "TraderTraitor" is trying to quickly protect its newfound loot. First of all, they want to turn any Stablecoin into assets that cannot be frozen, like Ether (ETH). From there, the group is using automation to create LOTS of new wallets to filter small amounts of crypto, so as not to trigger alarms for moving assets worth a bazillion dollars. From there, launderers want to move the money across networks like Ethereum to Bitcoin then pull it from a mixed pool with a bunch of other people's assets. The goal: make the crypto's origins hazy. "TraderTraitor" is moving fast. On Tuesday, Elliptic reported the group has made more than 40,000 transactions, creating a new wallet every 25 seconds.
One interesting detail: Binance has promised to make customers whole , but investors have already pulled billions from the exchange.

What to know: This week, gold fell below $4,000 per ounce after hitting nearly $5,600 per ounce in January. It's typically seen as a safe-haven asset, which is why investors were shoveling money into it earlier this year. As you know, things have been a bit volatile from the Iran War to the criminal probe into the Federal Reserve chair. But today, there's still economic uncertainty, no? The war with Iran rages on. So why are gold prices falling? I took my question to Planet Money co-host Jeff Guo to find out. I asked him: could gold be going down because Treasury bond yields are up? That could mean there are MORE reliable ways to make money.
Why is gold going down? : Our answer, courtesy of Jeff Guo!

Jeff: I think you are right that rising Treasury yields are the story. As you know, gold tends to be seen as a "safe" asset and an inflation hedge; but the problem is that gold doesn't earn any income/interest on its own. Meanwhile, you could buy a 10 year TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) bond right now that does earn income, above and beyond inflation. Sure, the Iran war is a source of political instability that might drive investors toward gold. But the main effect of the war so far seems to be raising the price of oil. And higher oil prices are one of the factors pushing interest rates up, making bonds more attractive relative to gold.
What the election means for data centers - Washington Post

What to know: People do not want data centers and the election left us with numbers to prove it. Apparently voters either BANNED or placed restrictions on data centers in at least 38 jurisdictions across the country. The numbers within the ballot measures were fascinating. It's also notable that Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, ran on a platform of reining in data centers. She called for a moratorium on new projects and pushing for more aggressive protections on both ratepayers and the environment. A Democrat hasn't been governor in Texas in more than 30 years.

Why it matters: All this local opposition could actually make an impact on what big tech wants to do. Local opposition has already made a difference in data center world. S&P Global has tracked projects nationwide and found more than 146 were delayed or canceled through early August. 75% of those were tied to local opposition. Several big tech companies are dropping contract provisions that have drawn the public's ire – one that keeps early phases of data center projects a secret, for example. We will be keeping an eye on this.

title_en: What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina
title_zh: 北卡罗来纳州的蓝浪是什么样子
summary: Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats in North Carolina. The surprising results were just one part of the blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times.
summary_zh: 民主党在北卡罗来纳州推翻了共和党控制的五个国会席位。这些令人惊讶的结果只是瑞士蓝色浪潮的一部分
body_en: What the blue wave looked like in North Carolina Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats in North Carolina. The surprising results were just one part of the blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times.
Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats in North Carolina. The surprising results were just one part of the blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times.

To North Carolina now, where Democrats have flipped five Republican-held congressional seats. That's according to race calls by The Associated Press. Democrats also held on to a redistricted seat. Most of those races, they were not even considered competitive going into Tuesday's election. The remaining congressional races in the state are still too close to call. The surprising results were just one part of the big blue wave in a swing state that President Trump won three times. Colin Campbell covers politics for member station WUNC. He's on the line from Raleigh. Hey there, Colin.
KELLY: OK, tell me more about North Carolina's congressional map.

CAMPBELL: So Republicans currently hold 10 of the state's 14 House seats, and last year, state lawmakers gerrymandered those maps even more to try to unseat Democrat Don Davis in the state's northeastern corner. That didn't actually happen. AP called that race for Davis today. It was one of the most expensive races in the country and one we'd all been watching along with the western North Carolina district where Democrat Jamie Ager flipped an open GOP seat by a pretty big margin.

But most of us weren't paying close attention at all to the nine districts with Republican incumbents on the ballot. All of them won by big margins two years ago, but we learned today that Congressman Tim Moore, Richard Hudson, Brad Knott and Addison McDowell all lost their seats to little-known Democrats. Hudson's particularly notable because he's actually the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. That's the campaign operation for the House GOP.
KELLY: And then there are four other Republican incumbents in North Carolina's delegation. Where do things stand for them?

CAMPBELL: None of their races have been called just yet. Three have narrow leads, but the state is still in the process of counting provisional and absentee ballots, so those numbers could change. Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx is currently just 99 votes behind her Democratic opponent. She's been in office since 2005, also chairs the House Rules Committee. All four of those races could be headed to recounts, and under our state law here, that process won't actually start until after November 13.

KELLY: So next week. So, you know, the question we've been asking for a couple of days now has been - how did Republicans manage to do so poorly? We're asking that in a lot of states. My question to you - how did Republicans do so poorly in a state where they had effectively drawn the map to favor their party?

CAMPBELL: A lot of it is the national environment. They just weren't expecting this big of a wave when they drew these maps and tried to figure out the optimal number. But North Carolina's U.S. Senate race also played a role. Former Governor Roy Cooper had such a big polling lead in that race that national Republican groups pulled all of their advertising for their candidate, Michael Whatley, moved that money to other states like Kansas in the final weeks. Most of the other Republicans here were actually relying on that spending to drive voter turnout in their races, and some of the congressional incumbents started running their own TV ads just in the final weeks of the campaign but looks like that was too little too late. Whatley ended up with less than 40% of the vote. He was Trump's pick to run for the seat but never really won over the Republican base here.
KELLY: Other things we should know about how the Blue wave broke there in North Carolina?

CAMPBELL: Democrats here easily won the state for the state Supreme Court, and they won a majority in the state House for the first time since 2008. They're pretty close to a tie in the state Senate too, which, if that happens, would be broken by the lieutenant governor who happens to be a Democrat. That's going to give Democratic Governor Josh Stein a lot more power next year, and he wants to make some redistricting reforms. Republicans, of course, still have some influence. So yesterday, he called on the two parties to come together and work on the affordability issues that dominated the election.

JOSH STEIN: What the voters want us to do is listen to what happened last night and focus on that. They want us to work for them and not be focused on reflecting pools or ballrooms or triumphal arches. They want a government that is worrying about their lives, the fact that gas has shot through the roof in price, that electricity bills are going up.
KELLY: All right, Democratic Governor Josh Stein in that reporting there from Colin Campbell, who covers North Carolina politics for member station WUNC. Thank you, Colin.

title_zh: 纽森宣布将为加州死囚减刑
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor says at 548 people, it's the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.
summary_zh: 加州州长加文·纽瑟姆宣布，他将对该州死囚区的所有囚犯进行减刑。州长说有 548 人，
body_en: Newsom announces he will commute sentences of inmates on California's death row California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor says at 548 people, it's the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he's commuting the sentences of all inmates on the state's Death Row. The governor says at 548 people, it's the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.

California Governor Gavin Newsom announced today that he is commuting all 548 death sentences on the books in his state. He is reducing all of the sentences to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The governor says California's death row is the largest in the Western hemisphere. Now, this action comes during a renewed national debate about capital punishment, following the recent botched execution attempt of a woman convicted of murder in Tennessee and also following the Trump administration's talk of livestreaming an execution at Fort Hood. That proposal was later rejected by President Trump. Scott Shafer of member station KQED is following the California governor's action today and joins us now. Hi, Scott.
CHANG: OK, so how did Governor Newsom explain his reasons for taking this step?

SHAFER: Well, the governor has been thinking about this for a long time now. He signaled on his podcast last month that he was framing it as a rocking chair test, meaning - how would he feel when he's old and sitting in a rocking chair reflecting on his life? He clearly sees opposition to the death penalty as, you know, kind of fundamental to his values and his faith. So it was pretty clear this was going to happen. They waited until just after the election to do it. He issued a statement today explaining why he did this, and among other things, he said the death penalty is a failure. You know, we haven't had an execution in California in 20 years. He also said it's immoral for the state to murder somebody and that it isn't applied fairly anyway.
CHANG: OK. Well, Newsom had already put death sentences on hold, right? So explain how this step today differs from that earlier step.

SHAFER: Yeah, he issued that moratorium on executions two months after he became governor - that was 2019 - dismantled the execution chamber at San Quentin prison, and they moved death row inmates from San Quentin to other maximum-security prisons across the state. So in some ways, this is symbolic since there aren't any executions on the horizon anyway. But by commuting these hundreds of sentences, it might give momentum to death penalty opponents in other states, you know, to lobby governors there to do something similar. And I should emphasize, Ailsa, that Newsom's actions today do not eliminate the death penalty in California. Only the voters can do that.
CHANG: Right. OK, so what's been the reaction so far there in California? Like, what have victims had to say about this?

SHAFER: Well, Newsom met with many crime victims before he issued the moratorium on executions back in 2019. Needless to say, those are very hard conversations, very raw. He met with many of those folks again over the past months as he considered this decision, and in his statement today, he sort of spoke to them saying, commuting these death sentences could resurface excruciating memories for them. He does not dismiss that in any way. He also said that he didn't want to pick and choose which death sentences to commute and which to let stand, saying that that could inadvertently create two classes of murder victims, which he did not want to do.

CHANG: OK. Well, you suggest that today's actions by Newsom were pretty anticipated. I mean, Newsom is often mentioned as a possible candidate for president in 2028. So talk about the political context here for this move.

SHAFER: Yeah, this was anticipated, for those of us paying attention to it. He waited until after Tuesday's election, so it wouldn't become an issue. And as to the politics, you know, there are certainly some advisers in Newsom's political orbit who urged him not to do it as he gets ready to run for president. But one of his advisers said that when he did this seven years ago, Newsom never asked to see any polls or look at anything related to the politics of it. And across the country, Gallup has been polling on this for decades, and support for the death penalty is at its lowest point in decades. So it's not really clear Newsom will pay a political price for this.
CHANG: That is Scott Shafer from member station KQED in San Francisco. Thank you, Scott.

title_en: How Abdul El-Sayed actually did with Jewish voters
title_zh: 阿卜杜勒·赛义德实际上是如何对待犹太选民的
summary: Yes, he ran behind. In an interview, the senator-elect acknowledged Israel was a source of disagreement, but said he’s not changing his position.
summary_zh: 是的，他跑到了后面。在接受采访时，当选参议员承认以色列是分歧的根源，但表示他不会改变立场。
body_en: Abdul El-Sayed ran well behind other Michigan Democrats in places with more Jewish voters, according to a detailed POLITICO analysis of precinct-level results.

Statewide, the progressive senator-elect only ran two points behind Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson, getting 52.5% of the vote compared to her 54.5%. But the gap was much larger in heavily Jewish communities: In Huntington Woods, a Detroit suburb that is roughly two-thirds Jewish, El-Sayed ran nearly 15 points behind Benson, getting 65.3% of the vote compared to Benson’s 80%.
In West Bloomfield, the site of the March synagogue attack that shook the Senate primary and a town where roughly a quarter of residents are Jewish, El-Sayed ran 8.8 points behind Benson.

El-Sayed faced blowback from some Jewish Democrats during his campaign, particularly over his calls to end U.S. military support to Israel and his remarks after the synagogue attack that “hurt people hurt people,” for which he later apologized .
El-Sayed, who will be the first Muslim senator in U.S. history, told POLITICO on Wednesday that he hoped he could “earn support” from Jewish voters who hadn’t backed him in this election.

“One of the big issues of disagreement that kept showing up when it came to the Jewish community was my position on Israel,” El-Sayed said. “I'm not going to change my position, but …I intend to lead on all the issues that we agree on — whether it's the right to a union or the right to health care, clean air, clean water, or religious pluralism, and respect for the Constitution — and I hope that over time I can earn [their] support on those issues.”

El-Sayed had worked to make inroads with Jewish voters over the course of his campaign, pledging to stand up to antisemitism and for Jewish safety. Still, some Jewish leaders and activists in the state urged voters to blank their ballots in the Senate race, or back Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers.

His former Democratic primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, also switched her endorsement from El-Sayed to Rogers days before the election, citing concerns over antisemitism and the Democrat and his allies’ views and rhetoric around Israel. She pointed to an ad put out by a prominent El-Sayed supporter tying high grocery prices to U.S. aid to Israel, which El-Sayed and his campaign distanced themselves from.

Jewish voters, who make up roughly 1.4% of the Michigan electorate, have historically backed Democrats by large margins. But disagreements over support for Israel and how the party should respond to rising antisemitism are testing that voting bloc — both in Michigan and across the country.
A poll of Jewish early voters in the state found that a majority still backed El-Sayed, but roughly one in four who had supported Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024 switched to back Rogers.

With Michigan in Democrats’ early primary window for 2028, El-Sayed said his statewide win showed voters were aligned with his positioning on Israel — and that he hopes the next presidential nominee takes note.

“If you want to be where the voters are, if you want to be on the side of peace and on the side of justice and transparency, I believe that that is around holding Israel accountable to its war crimes and on making sure our tax dollars get used to do good things here rather than bad things somewhere else,” he said.

In a post-election memo , El-Sayed’s campaign touted an outside analysis finding that he only ran slightly behind Slotkin’s 2024 performance in predominantly Jewish precincts. The memo also noted he was outspent heavily in both the primary and general elections, including by “MAGA billionaires, AIPAC, Elon Musk, and corporate interests determined to elect candidates who would defend the status quo.”

But he won in a blue wave while Slotkin, who is Jewish, overcame a tough year. El-Sayed’s margins were far better than Slotkin’s numbers across nearly all of the state, suggesting Jewish voters moved in the opposite direction of most Michiganders.

On the other hand, El-Sayed particularly surged in areas with more Muslim voters, who make up roughly 2.4% of Michigan’s electorate. In Dearborn, for example, he won 82.5% of the vote compared to 78.7% for Benson. Two years ago, Slotkin won 41.4% in the city while former Vice President Kamala Harris received just 36.3% of the vote.

Lansing Mayor Andy Schor, a Jewish Democrat who supported Stevens in the primary and did not endorse El-Sayed, said he was unsurprised by that split screen. He expressed hope about El-Sayed’s relationship with the Jewish community going forward, but also said Jewish leaders should continue to raise their concerns to the incoming senator.
“Everybody has to keep talking to him. His views aren’t going to change, and we know what they are,” Schor said. But, “I hope he’s open to hearing the concerns of some of his constituents.”

Nonnegotiable Michigan, a group of Jewish activists that pushed El-Sayed on issues of Jewish safety and Israel, also said in a postelection statement that it was “prepared to work with” El-Sayed “even as we continue to hold elected leaders accountable when antisemitism enters our politics or political discourse.”
El-Sayed made clear he has no plans to change his views on Israel, but said he will be straight with voters — and that he’ll “show up for you when you need me” regardless of their differences.

“With me, what you see is what you get. And I've never once gone and told somebody that I was anything but what I am,” El-Sayed said Wednesday. “We're going to disagree. I'm going to be honest, specific and direct. And over time, I hope that I can earn support for leading on the issues on which I hope to lead and [by] serving everybody.”
body_zh: 根据《政治》杂志对选区一级结果的详细分析，阿卜杜勒·赛义德在犹太选民较多的地方远远落后于其他密歇根州民主党人。
在全州范围内，这位进步派当选参议员仅落后民主党州长当选人乔斯林·本森 (Jocelyn Benson) 两分，她获得了 52.5% 的选票，而她的得票率为 54.5%。但在犹太人口较多的社区，这种差距要大得多：在大约三分之二是犹太人的底特律郊区亨廷顿伍兹，埃尔-赛义德落后本森近 15 个百分点，获得了 65.3% 的选票，而本森只有 80%。
在西布卢姆菲尔德，三月犹太教堂袭击事件震惊了参议院初选，该镇约有四分之一的居民是犹太人，埃尔-赛义德的支持率落后本森 8.8 个百分点。
埃尔赛义德在竞选期间遭到了一些犹太民主党人的反击，特别是他呼吁结束美国对以色列的军事支持，以及他在犹太教堂袭击后发表的“伤人伤人”的言论，他后来为此道歉。
埃尔-赛义德将成为美国历史上第一位穆斯林参议员，他周三告诉《政治》杂志，他希望自己能够“赢得”在这次选举中不支持他的犹太选民的支持。
“当谈到犹太社区时，不断出现的重大分歧问题之一是我对以色列的立场，”埃尔赛义德说。 “我不会改变我的立场，但是……我打算在我们同意的所有问题上发挥领导作用——无论是工会权还是医疗保健权、清洁空气、清洁水或宗教多元化，以及尊重宪法——我希望随着时间的推移，我能够在这些问题上赢得[他们]的支持。”
埃尔-赛义德在竞选过程中一直努力争取犹太选民的支持，承诺抵制反犹太主义并维护犹太人的安全。尽管如此，该州的一些犹太领袖和活动人士仍敦促选民在参议院竞选中留白选票，或支持共和党前众议员迈克·罗杰斯。
他的前民主党主要竞争对手、众议员海莉·史蒂文斯也在选举前几天将她的支持从埃尔·赛义德转为罗杰斯，理由是对反犹太主义以及民主党及其盟友围绕以色列的观点和言论的担忧。她指出，一位著名的赛义德支持者发布的一则广告将高杂货价格与美国对以色列的援助挂钩，赛义德和他的竞选团队与此保持距离。
犹太选民约占密歇根州选民的 1.4%，历来以大幅优势支持民主党。但在支持以色列以及该党应如何应对日益高涨的反犹太主义方面存在的分歧正在考验这个投票集团——无论是在密歇根州还是在全国各地。
对该州犹太早期选民的一项民意调查发现，大多数人仍然支持埃尔-赛义德，但大约四分之一的 2024 年支持参议员埃丽莎·斯洛特金的人转而支持罗杰斯。
密歇根州正处于民主党 2028 年的早期初选窗口，埃尔-赛义德表示，他在全州范围内的胜利表明选民与他对以色列的立场一致，他希望下一任总统候选人能够注意到这一点。
他说：“如果你想站在选民的立场上，如果你想站在和平一边，站在正义和透明一边，我认为那就是让以色列对其战争罪行负责，并确保我们的税款在这里用来做好事，而不是在其他地方做坏事。”
在一份选举后的备忘录中，埃尔·赛义德的竞选团队吹捧了一项外部分析结果，该分析发现，他在 2024 年在犹太人占主导地位的选区的表现仅略落后于斯洛特金。备忘录还指出，他在初选和大选中的支出都超过了他，其中包括“MAGA 亿万富翁、AIPAC、埃隆·马斯克和决心选举捍卫现状的候选人的企业利益集团”。
但他在蓝色浪潮中获胜，而犹太人斯洛特金则克服了艰难的一年。在几乎全州范围内，埃尔-赛义德的支持率远高于斯洛特金的支持率，这表明犹太选民的投票方向与大多数密歇根人相反。
另一方面，埃尔-赛义德在穆斯林选民较多的地区尤其飙升，穆斯林选民约占密歇根州选民的 2.4%。例如，在迪尔伯恩，他赢得了 82.5% 的选票，而本森赢得了 78.7% 的选票。两年前，斯洛特金在该市赢得了 41.4% 的选票，而前副总统卡马拉·哈里斯 (Kamala Harris) 仅获得 36.3% 的选票。
兰辛市市长安迪·肖尔（Andy Schor）是一名犹太民主党人，他在初选中支持史蒂文斯，但不支持埃尔·赛义德。他表示，他对分屏并不感到惊讶。他对埃尔赛义德与犹太社区的关系未来发展表示希望，但也表示犹太领导人应继续向即将上任的参议员提出他们的担忧。
“每个人都必须继续与他交谈。他的观点不会改变，我们知道这些观点是什么，”肖尔说。但是，“我希望他愿意倾听一些选民的担忧。”
不可谈判的密歇根州是一个在犹太安全和以色列问题上推动埃尔赛义德的犹太活动家组织，该组织也在一份选举后声明中表示，它“准备与”埃尔赛义德合作，“即使当反犹太主义进入我们的政治或政治话语时，我们仍将继续追究民选领导人的责任”。
埃尔-赛义德明确表示，他不打算改变对以色列的看法，但表示他将坦诚地对待选民，并且无论选民之间存在分歧，他都会“在你们需要我的时候出现在你们身边”。
“对我来说，所见即所得。我从来没有告诉过别人我不是我，”埃尔-赛义德周三说道。 “我们会不同意。我会诚实、具体和直接。随着时间的推移，我希望我能够赢得支持，以领导我希望领导和服务所有人的问题。”

title_en: 3 charged with using AI to steal some $129 million from companies
title_zh: 3 charged with using AI to steal some $129 million from companies
summary: Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted, prosecutors say.
summary_zh: Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted, prosecutors say.
body_en: 3 allegedly used AI to steal some $129 million from companies by impersonating executives and lawyers - CBS News

New York — Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted on charges of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, prosecutors said Thursday .

Over more than a year and a half, Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, targeted thousands of companies across the world in their AI scheme, according to the indictment filed in a U.S. District Court in New York.

Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida, according to court documents.
The defendants, from Spain, the U.K., Israel and the United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering, according to the indictment.

Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit didn't immediately respond to an email requesting comment. It wasn't clear whether Hazan had an attorney. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York didn't immediately respond to a voicemail left by The Associated Press.
The three were arrested between June and September — Soall and Hazan in Spain and Sheetrit in the U.K. Extradition requests for all three are pending.
In 2008, Hazan was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

The trio, who have nicknames that include "Rocky Balboa," "Superman Cash" and "Fat Boy," often targeted the companies' accounting departments. They would send an email purporting to be from the CEO and ask for help with a confidential financial transaction, according to court documents.
They would also coordinate a phone or video call where the defendants used AI to mimic the voice and sometimes the image of the CEO, according to the indictment.
The defendants would then tell them to contact an attorney at a major law firm, who the group was also ready to impersonate, according to court documents.

Soall mainly impersonated attorneys from the U.K. and had a "handwritten script titled 'Lawyer Call' that he utilized to make himself seem like a real attorney when speaking with and defrauding victims," according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

The impersonated attorney would tell the employee to wire large payments to bank accounts across the world, according to court documents. The funds were then converted into cryptocurrency to try to conceal where they came from and then distributed to the trio and others involved, according to court documents.
FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. said the case shows how advanced technology can be used to commit large-scale fraud.

"As criminals continue to weaponize emerging technologies, the FBI remains committed to rapidly adapting our capabilities to identify, investigate and disrupt those who seek to harm New Yorkers and businesses operating in our communities," he said in a statement.
If convicted, the defendants face a maximum sentence of 20 years, except for aggravated identity theft, which has a maximum sentence of two years, according to the attorney's office.

title_en: Grim details emerge after woman and daughter killed by bear
title_zh: Grim details emerge after woman and daughter killed by bear
summary: The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain and the grizzly bear's behavior.
summary_zh: The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain and the grizzly bear's behavior.
body_en: Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.

When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.

Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found . The search was now a tragic recovery effort.

The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 3 to 4 kilometers (1.8 to 2.4 miles) from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.

Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials have set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. They also are not sure whether more than one bear was involved.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said the killings were triggering for the families who were traumatized by last year's attack.

"Our community is still healing," he said, adding that they've imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. "Our priority is to ensure they're safe and ensure our community is supported."
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear's behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.

Searchers found his niece's remains in a bear cache - a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
"Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult," he said.

By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
"There's no obvious body to identify," he said. "The coroner's investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs."
Balcarras was comfortable in challenging environments

Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.

Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was "the central organizing person in our family," Matt Balcarras said.

"In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids," Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.

"She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies," he said. "She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They've lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades."

title_en: LeBron James took a risk going to the 76ers this offseason. So far, it’s paying off.
title_zh: LeBron James took a risk going to the 76ers this offseason. So far, it’s paying off.
summary: James, who switched teams for the fourth time in free agency over the summer, has helped lead the Philadelphia 76ers to the hottest start in the NBA.
summary_zh: James, who switched teams for the fourth time in free agency over the summer, has helped lead the Philadelphia 76ers to the hottest start in the NBA.
body_en: When his agent, Rich Paul, revealed on a whiteboard the teams likeliest to sign him in the summer, LeBron James appeared to be choosing among five contenders after he entered free agency: the Philadelphia 76ers, the Miami Heat, the Minnesota Timberwolves, the Denver Nuggets and the Cleveland Cavaliers.
James, in something of a surprise, picked the 76ers. And through the (very) early part of this season, he appears to have chosen wisely.

Philadelphia is 8-1 after a win over the Detroit Pistons on Wednesday night. The 76ers have the most wins in the NBA entering Friday, and their high-powered starting five has jelled quickly to form an undeniable title contender.
In addition to signing James, Philly traded for swingman Jaylen Brown in the offseason, forming a starting five of James, Brown, Tyrese Maxey, V.J. Edgecombe and Joel Embiid.
Those five players have combined for 36 All-Star selections, five MVP awards and five Finals MVP awards. So it’s perhaps unsurprising the group has been great together on the floor.

In 77 minutes together across five games, the Sixers’ starting five has outscored opponents by 15 points. Philadelphia’s opening quintet is dominating defensively, holding opponents to only 95.4 points per 100 possessions. (For context, the league’s best defense entering Thursday was holding opponents to 103 points per 100 possessions.)

“Our defense is going to be our identity,” James said Wednesday after the win over the Pistons. “We have a lot of scoring. We know that from individuals. We’re still figuring out that side of the floor out on the offensive side. Defensively, that’s where we are going to make our mark.”

James has meshed well with all of his co-stars so far. All two-man lineups featuring a combo of James plus one of Maxey, Brown, Embiid and Edgecombe have outscored opponents through the team’s first nine games.
Playing on a roster loaded with talent, James has seemingly been happy to become one of the best role players in the NBA.

Through his first seven games, James is averaging 15.7 points, 7.4 rebounds and 7.4 assists a night. His scoring average, field-goal attempts per game (13.1) and free-throw attempts (4.4) are all on pace to be career-low marks. While James hasn’t necessarily made up for the dip in efficiency — his 45.7% shooting from the field would be his lowest since his rookie season — his willingness to take a back seat has helped Maxey in particular.
The speedy guard is averaging 28.0 points on a career-best 48.6% shooting.

“It was a long offseason for me,” Maxey said this month. “I worked on my passing. I worked on my isolation scoring and my late-game scoring. I wanted to be able to come back with a move that I could get to late in games, because I knew we were going to need it. I knew we would need it, and I knew that I would be ready to do it.”
Said Brown: “Max has been leading the way, 100%. He’s been here. This is his team.”
Everyone has sacrificed to some degree, including Embiid, who admitted he was struggling adapting to his new role as his shot attempts diminish.

“My mindset is really on whenever I have the ball, make plays,” Embiid said. “Make the game easy for all these guys. Making the right play over and over, setting screens, get Tyrese as open as possible, Bron, all these guys.”
How does this compare to previous James teams?
Typically, when James joins a new team, it takes a little while for things to come together.

The 2010-11 Miami Heat, for example, started only 6-4 in their first 10 games. The team was only 9-8 after 17 games, when James famously bumped into coach Erik Spoelstra during the team’s eighth loss.
The 2014-15 Cleveland Cavaliers were worse, starting 5-5 when James returned home. The Cavs struggled until January, hovering around .500 until they embarked on a 12-game winning streak midseason.

The 2018-19 Los Angeles Lakers started the season 4-6 and eventually missed the playoffs after James sustained a groin injury late in the year. Much of that team was turned over the following offseason after the Lakers acquired Anthony Davis.

title_zh: Normal Americans taught an election lesson — again

body_en: Voters were unambiguous on Tuesday: Don't B.S. us. Don't say you'll lower prices and end wars and corruption, then do the opposite. It's really that simple.
This isn't so different from when Americans told Democrats not to B.S. them about Joe Biden's health, or about the words they should use, or social behaviors they should adopt.
Why it matters: Most Americans agree broadly on most things, most of the time. They want competent politicians to focus on issues that meaningfully impact their lives.
Like clockwork, every two years, Americans feel the party in power fails to deliver this — so they punish the incumbents at the polls.
Politicians and some journalists tend to treat the American people as dopes and dupes who don't get what's happening in front of their faces.

Tuesday's midterms, which will live in history as a Watergate-level reset for democracy, show that voters were paying attention and hit a boiling point. They didn't hide it. Polls consistently showed that all they really care about is rising inflation, job insecurity, ending the war, and stopping the rampant corruption.
This was a repudiation of overreach, incompetence and corruption. People will tolerate it in small doses, but eventually reject it.
In an age when people trust institutions less all the time , our institutions held. Courts restrained executive-branch excess. The press kept doing its job. Voters did theirs.
But for all the hand-wringing that America is crumbling, that democracy is fading, or elections are eroding, the system worked. Remember: most Americans are normal and resilient.
We should celebrate that. Despite it all, America works.

For years, we've been reminding you about the power of Normal America : The vast majority of people — including our siblings, who are scattered from Oshkosh to Oregon — don't marinate in cable news, obsess about X or wake up thinking about Washington.
They volunteer, they give to good causes, they'll help you in a pinch.
They're good, they're fair ... and they're smart.

Between the lines: That's Normal America. Sometimes when we're making a tough call about journalism or business, we ask ourselves: "What would the person at the bar think?" It's a useful, clarifying proxy for: What would seem on the level through the lens of common sense and plain fairness?

The person at the bar, and the voter in the booth, didn't want their soccer coach deported, didn't want their business to crumble because of a war of choice that's dragging on and on, didn't want the president's family and friends to enrich themselves while Normal America was wheezing.
What we're watching: Democrats will be tempted and pressured to overreach. If they overinterpret their mandate the way Republicans did, they'll be punished, like clockwork.

Here's what Republicans and Democrats will do if they're smart: Watch Texas. A seemingly impenetrable red state turned all blue, from the U.S. Senate to the governor's office to the state legislature. If Democrats can keep Texas, Republicans have no path to the presidency.

Look at what happened in those southern border counties in Texas. These were the people who demanded tighter borders and punished Democrats when they wouldn't listen. But they're the same people who are saying stop with the thuggery and targeting of nonviolent people. Republicans were obliterated in those areas for not listening.

Then look to the Texas suburbs, where you have many more traditional Republicans and moderate Democrats. They looked at Ken Paxton and said he's simply not on the level, even if they might agree with him on a lot of ideas. Corruption is never a good look. Enabling it and elevating it is even worse.
The bottom line: This remains a 50-50 nation — a simple fact that every party and power instantly, constantly ignores. Once again, Normal Americans spoke: Ignore or B.S. them at your peril.

title_zh: Scoop: Trump to keep fundraising, hoping to retain political muscle

summary_zh: President Trump has told advisers that he plans to keep raising money for his political operation — a move aimed at salvaging his clout after the GOP's midterm debacle. Why it matters: Maintaining a political organization — either his existing MAGA Inc. super
body_en: President Trump has told advisers that he plans to keep raising money for his political operation — a move aimed at salvaging his clout after the GOP's midterm debacle.

Why it matters: Maintaining a political organization — either his existing MAGA Inc. super PAC or one to be created — would give Trump a vehicle to try to influence elections in 2028 and beyond, including the next presidential contest.

It also would give Trump a way to pressure GOP lawmakers who consider breaking with him as the unpopular president enters his lame-duck era and Democrats prepare congressional investigations into his administration.
Trump's MAGA Inc. enforced party discipline during the 2026 primary campaigns when it helped defeat Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie (R), an outspoken Trump critic.
Zoom in: MAGA Inc. has been the centerpiece of Trump's political operation during his second term, raising nearly $450 million since the beginning of 2025.
The group received massive checks from cryptocurrency and AI industry donors, along with Republican megadonors such as Elon Musk and Miriam Adelson.
Trump has hosted high-dollar fundraising dinners at Mar-a-Lago and his golf club in Sterling, Va., drawing business leaders eager to curry favor with the president.

Some donors subsequently benefited from administration decisions. The New York Times reported that a medical products company whose executives and affiliates gave $5 million to MAGA Inc. benefited from an administration decision to delay Medicare reimbursement restrictions, for example.
By the numbers: MAGA Inc. spent more than $400 million on the midterms, making it one of the election's biggest spending forces, according to a source familiar with the totals.
The massive investment failed to prevent Republicans from losing control of Congress amid voter anger over Trump's war on Iran, high prices and corruption concerns.
As of Oct. 14, MAGA Inc. had more than $164 million in the bank, though it spent tens of millions more on TV and digital advertising in the campaign's final weeks so it's unclear how much remains.
The group invested aggressively in traditionally safe GOP seats that had become competitive, helping some Republicans survive, according to party operatives.
Yes, but: Raising money could become much harder with Democrats controlling Congress and major donors beginning to look turning their attention toward 2028.
Republicans say Trump's diminished political clout will make it harder to attract the enormous checks that have flowed into MAGA Inc.
The prospect of congressional investigations into alleged pay-for-play arrangements involving donors to Trump's political operation could further discourage contributions.
Technology executives who contributed heavily to the group may increasingly turn to Democrats, while major Republican donors shift their attention to prospective 2028 presidential candidates.
What they're saying: A MAGA Inc. spokesperson declined to comment. White House spokespeople didn't respond to a request for comment.

The Trump administration has escalated its economic campaign against Cuba

The Trump administration on Thursday escalated its economic campaign against Cuba , issuing a determination that clears the path for U.S. sanctions on several crucial sectors of the island's economy while also targeting Chinese-based suppliers to Havana's military forces.

The sanctions are part of a larger effort by President Donald Trump and his allies to force political change in Havana even as the country continues to grapple with a deepening economic and energy crisis that has suffocated its population.
With the new penalties the State Department is expanding its reach to target new sectors of Cuba's economy, including electronics, manufacturing, marine and technology.

“Cuba’s ruling elite is hoarding the island’s energy, shipping, and technology resources for its own enrichment, leaving the Cuban people to contend with blackouts, shortages, and a stagnant economy,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

In total, eight entities and two individuals were targeted, including China National Electronic Import and Export Company and Beijing H & C Technologies, two China-based companies that the U.S. is accusing of procuring weapons and selling surveillance and security equipment to the Cuban government.

Last week, the U.N. General Assembly condemned the U.S. economic embargo of Cuba for the 34th year. But the U.S. campaign to influence the outcome led a number of countries to vote against the resolution or sit out the decision for the first time.

特朗普政府周四升级了针对古巴的经济行动，发布了一项决定，为美国对该岛经济的几个关键部门实施制裁扫清了道路，同时也针对哈瓦那军队的中国供应商。
这些制裁是唐纳德·特朗普总统及其盟友为迫使哈瓦那进行政治变革而做出的更大努力的一部分，尽管该国仍在努力应对日益严重的经济和能源危机，该危机已导致其民众窒息。
通过新的处罚措施，国务院正在扩大制裁范围，瞄准古巴经济的新领域，包括电子、制造、海洋和技术。
美国国务卿马可·卢比奥在一份声明中表示：“古巴的统治精英正在囤积岛上的能源、航运和技术资源，以谋取私利，使古巴人民面临停电、短缺和经济停滞的困境。”
总共有八个实体和两名个人成为攻击目标，其中包括中国电子进出口公司和北京宏创科技有限公司，美国指控这两家中国公司向古巴政府采购武器并向古巴政府出售监控和安全设备。
